title: When Parenting Gets Hard
subtitle: Prodigals, Doubt, Screens, and the Crises No One Prepped You For
blurb: Essays for the hardest parts of parenting, the prodigal, the child who doubts or walks away or comes out, special needs, single parenting, screens and phones, sex and identity, and grief.

chapters.title: Adoption Theology: What It Means to Be Chosen
chapters.summary: Adoption is not a lesser way to build a family. It is the metaphor the New Testament chose to describe how God brings us home. To adopt is to enact the gospel.
chapters.body:
Of all the images the New Testament reaches for to describe what God has done for us, one of the most striking is adoption. Not merely forgiveness, not merely rescue, but adoption, the deliberate act of taking someone who was not yours by birth and making them yours by choice, with all the rights and the inheritance and the name that belong to a child born into the house. Paul returns to this image again and again, and it is worth asking why. Why, of all the metaphors available, did the Spirit inspire the language of adoption to describe the deepest thing about our salvation?

I have watched families formed by adoption up close over many years of ministry, and I have come to believe that adoption is not a lesser or backup way of building a family, a plan B for those who could not do it the ordinary way. It is, if anything, the truer picture of what every family is meant to be, and the clearest earthly enactment of the gospel that I know. To adopt is not merely to add a child to a home. It is to preach, with your whole life, the way God brings the outsider in.

## The scandal of chosen belonging

We tend to romanticize biological connection, to treat the tie of blood as the deepest and most natural bond. And there is something real there. But the New Testament does something startling with the family. It relativizes blood. Jesus, asked about his mother and brothers, gestures to those who do the will of God and calls them his family. The community of faith is repeatedly described as a family constituted not by biology but by covenant, by the choosing love of God who calls strangers his children.

Adoption sits at the heart of this reordering. It declares that belonging does not require biology, that a bond chosen and covenanted is as real and as unbreakable as a bond by blood. This is a scandal to a culture that worships genetic connection, and it is meant to be, because it mirrors the deeper scandal of the gospel, that God did not wait for us to be his by nature but chose us, adopted us, brought the outsider into the household and made no distinction between the natural-born and the adopted heir.

> Adoption declares that belonging is not something you are born into but something you are chosen for. That is not a lesser belonging. In the gospel, it is the deepest one.

In the Roman world in which Paul wrote, adoption was not a marginal or sentimental arrangement. It was a legal act of enormous weight, by which a person, often an adult, was transferred entirely into a new family, given a new name, made heir to a new estate, released from all former debts and obligations. The adopted son was not a lesser son. Under the law, he was in some respects more securely a son than one born into the family, because his sonship rested on a deliberate act of choosing that could not be undone. When Paul reached for this image to describe our salvation, he reached for the strongest picture of belonging his culture possessed.

## Chosen, not settled for

One of the wounds that can attach to an adopted child is the fear of being a second choice, a substitute for the child that could not be, a consolation for a loss. And an adoptive parent must labor against this fear with everything they have, because it is a lie that can poison a life. The truth the gospel offers is precisely the opposite. In adoption, the child is not settled for. The child is chosen.

Think of what God does in adopting us. He does not settle for us because his real children failed to materialize. He deliberately, joyfully, at enormous cost, chooses to make us his own. The language Paul uses is the language of delight, of purpose, of a love that predates our existence and reaches out to claim us not as a fallback but as an intention. To adopt a child in this spirit is to say to them, with your whole life, you were not a substitute. You were the intention. I chose you, and choosing is not less than birthing. In some ways it is more.

There is a particular grief that often precedes adoption, a grief of infertility or loss, and it would be dishonest to pretend that grief plays no part in the story. But the grief that precedes an adoption does not make the child a consolation prize, any more than the grief that precedes a remarriage makes the new spouse a substitute. A parent can have arrived at adoption through sorrow and still choose the child before them with a wholeness and a delight that owes nothing to the sorrow that came before. The child is not the patch over an old wound. The child is a new and complete love, chosen for their own sake.

And there is a deep comfort in this for the child who fears they were second best. The God who adopts us did not do so because his plan for a perfect creation had failed and we were what was left. He chose us from before the foundation of the world, deliberately, with intention and delight, and the language Scripture uses for our adoption is language of purpose and joy, not of resignation. When an adoptive parent looks at their child and says, I did not settle for you, I chose you, and choosing you was one of the great intentions of my life, they are speaking to the child the very words God speaks to every one of us. The fear of being a substitute is answered not by a technique but by a truth, and the truth is that in the economy of grace, to be chosen is the highest form of belonging there is, higher even than to be born, because it rests on nothing but the deliberate love of the one who chose.

## Naming the loss honestly

And yet I would be dishonest, and I would fail the adopted, if I painted only the glory and ignored the grief. Adoption is built on loss. Before there is a joining, there is a separation. Before a child is welcomed into a new family, they have lost, in some form, the family of their origin. This loss is real, and it does not disappear because the adoption is loving. To pretend otherwise, to insist that the adopted child should feel only gratitude and never grief, is to add a second wound on top of the first.

The most loving adoptive families I have known are the ones that can hold both truths at once. They can celebrate the joy of the joining and honor the grief of the loss, without asking the child to choose between them. They do not treat the child's questions about their origins as a betrayal. They do not require the child to be grateful in a way that suppresses their sorrow. They make room for the whole story, the loss and the finding, the grief and the joy, because a child who is allowed to grieve their loss is a child who can eventually receive their belonging without the poison of forced gratitude.

> An adopted child does not have to choose between grieving what they lost and receiving what they were given. The love that adopts them is large enough to hold both, and so must the family be.

## The gospel enacted, not just illustrated

What moves me most about adoption is that it does not merely illustrate the gospel. It enacts it. When a family takes in a child who was not theirs by birth, absorbs the cost, endures the difficulty, and loves the child into belonging, they are not putting on a play about what God did. They are doing, in miniature and in flesh, the very thing God did. They are absorbing the cost of another's brokenness and turning it into belonging. They are making the stranger a son, the outsider a daughter, the one who had no claim into an heir.

This is why adoption is one of the most theologically dense things a family can do. It is the gospel made visible, the abstract doctrine of our adoption in Christ pressed down into diapers and school forms and hard nights and the slow patient work of loving a child into trust. Every adoptive family that perseveres in love is preaching a sermon the watching world cannot ignore, a sermon about a God who welcomes the outsider and calls the stranger his own.

## The cost that mirrors the cross

We should not sentimentalize this. Adoption is costly, often far more costly than the glossy version acknowledges. Children who have known loss and disruption sometimes carry wounds that manifest as behavior a family did not anticipate. The love required is often a love that gives and gives and receives, for a long time, resistance and testing rather than gratitude. The child, having learned that attachment leads to loss, may fight the very belonging they most need, testing whether this family too will abandon them when it becomes hard.

And here again adoption mirrors the gospel, because this is exactly the love God shows us. He adopts us knowing we will test the belonging, knowing we will resist the love, knowing we will act out of our brokenness against the very One who welcomed us. And he does not withdraw. The love that adopts is a love that endures the testing, that stays through the resistance, that proves itself precisely by refusing to leave when leaving would be understandable. The cost of adoption is real, and it mirrors the cost of the cross, which is the cost God paid to make us his own.

The testing is not a sign that the adoption has failed. It is often a sign that it is working, that the child is beginning, however painfully, to believe the belonging is real enough to be tested. A child who has learned that love is fragile and abandonment is inevitable will push against a new love precisely to find out whether it too will break. Every act of resistance is, at bottom, a question, and the question is always the same: will you leave me too. And every time the adoptive parent absorbs the resistance without withdrawing, they answer the question, not with words, which the child has learned to distrust, but with presence, which is the only answer a wounded child can finally believe. The staying is the sermon. The refusal to leave, repeated across months and years of testing, slowly rewrites the deepest assumption the child carries, until one day they discover that they have come to trust a love they spent years trying to break, and could not.

## The identity questions that must be honored

An adopted child will, at some point, ask the questions that touch the deepest places. Who am I. Where did I come from. Why did they not keep me. Am I really yours. These questions can feel, to an adoptive parent, like a threat, as though the child's very asking is a rejection of the family that loves them. It is not. The questions are not a betrayal. They are the natural work of a person trying to understand their own story, and a child who is forbidden from asking them, or who senses that the questions wound their parents, learns to carry the questions in secret, where they fester.

The adoptive families I most admire have made their homes places where these questions are welcome, where the child's origins are spoken of with honesty and without threat, where curiosity about a birth family is met not with insecurity but with grace. This requires the adoptive parent to have done their own inner work, to be secure enough in the bond that they do not need the child to suppress their story in order to protect the parent's feelings. A child who is free to hold their whole story, the loss and the finding together, is a child who can integrate their identity rather than splitting it, and who can receive their belonging in the adoptive family precisely because they were never asked to deny where they came from. Security, not suppression, is what allows a child to be fully at home.

## What the church owes the adoptive family

If adoption is this central to the gospel, then the church ought to be its most fervent supporter, and not merely in sentiment but in substance. Adoptive families need community around them, support through the hard seasons, understanding when their children struggle in ways that are not the ordinary struggles. Too often the church celebrates the adoption at the beginning and disappears when the difficulty comes, leaving the family alone with challenges no one prepared them for.

The community that claims to believe in its own adoption by God should be the community that most surrounds those who adopt, that shares the burden, that provides the extended family every child needs. And it should be a community whose theology of belonging is deep enough that no adopted child in its midst ever feels like a second-class member of the family of God. Because in the gospel, there is no such thing. We were all adopted. Every one of us who belongs to God belongs by the same choosing love, the same welcome of the outsider, the same absorbing of cost that turns strangers into heirs. The adoptive family is not living out a special case of the gospel. They are living out its very center, and the rest of us are more like them than we know.

chapters.title: Death, Grief, and Children: How to Talk About Hard Things
chapters.summary: My son asked me if he was going to die, and I lied. I said not for a very long time. I do not know that. No parent knows that.
chapters.body:
My son asked me if he was going to die, and I lied. He was five, in the bath, and he asked it the way children ask everything, with no warning and full attention. And I said, not for a very long time, buddy. Then I changed the subject to something about a boat. I do not know that he will not die soon. No parent knows that. I said it because I could not bear the alternative, which was to sit in the bathwater with my son and tell him the truth, that everyone dies, that I do not control when, and that this is the one certainty I cannot protect him from.

We think we are protecting our children from death. We are usually protecting ourselves from their questions.

## The Death We Hide

Ours is the first culture in human history to keep children away from death almost entirely. For most of human history a child would see death by the time they were old enough to remember anything, a grandparent laid out in the front room, a sibling lost to fever, animals slaughtered for the table. Death was in the house. It was terrible, but it was known. We have moved death to hospitals and hospices and funeral homes, sanitized it, professionalized it, and in the process we have raised children who reach adulthood without ever having stood next to a body. We think this is mercy. It may be the opposite.

Because the child still knows. Children figure out death astonishingly early, usually around four or five, when they realize that dead is not a temporary condition, that the goldfish is not coming back, that this applies to grandparents and eventually to parents and eventually to them. They know. What they do not have, if we have hidden it, is any framework for what they know. They have the terror without the words and without the presence of an adult who will stay in the room while they feel it.

What we have actually done, by removing death from the ordinary landscape of childhood, is not spare our children from it but abandon them to it. The knowledge arrives anyway. It arrives through a dead pet, a news story, a classmate's grandmother, and it arrives to a child who has never once seen an adult handle death with steadiness and faith and tears all at the same time. So the child handles it alone, in the dark, at three in the morning, constructing whatever terrifying theory a five-year-old constructs when the biggest fact in the universe lands on them and the adults have quietly agreed not to discuss it. We did not protect them. We left them to face the largest thing there is without a guide.

## What Not to Say

The church has developed a set of phrases we deploy at children in grief, and most of them are quietly damaging. We tell a child that Grandpa went to sleep, and then we wonder why the child develops a terror of bedtime. We tell a child that God needed another angel, and we hand them a picture of a God who kills people because he is lonely, a God to be feared and resented rather than trusted. We tell a child that Grandma is in a better place, before the child has had a single second to be angry that she is not in this place, at this table, where she belongs.

> Every comforting lie we tell a grieving child is really a comfort we are giving ourselves. The child does not need the metaphor. We need it, because the truth is unbearable and the metaphor lets us leave the room.

The worst one, the one I have heard from well-meaning saints a hundred times, is do not cry, she is in heaven. This tells a grieving child that their grief is a theological error. That if they had more faith they would not be sad. It weaponizes the resurrection against the natural, God-given, entirely appropriate response of a heart that has lost someone it loves. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, a man he was about to raise from the dead. He knew Lazarus was coming back in five minutes and he still wept. If the certainty of resurrection did not cancel the tears of Christ, it does not get to cancel the tears of my child.

These phrases are not malicious. They come from adults who are themselves frightened, reaching for something to make the moment stop hurting, for the child and for themselves. But a frightened adult reaching for a comforting formula is exactly what a grieving child does not need. What the child needs is an adult who is not so frightened of death that they have to paper over it instantly, an adult who can say the true and terrible thing gently and then stay in the room while it lands. That adult is rare, because it requires the adult to have made some peace with death themselves, and most of us have not, and the phrases are how we hide that we have not.

## Grief Is Not the Enemy of Faith

Somewhere we absorbed the idea that a faithful Christian does not grieve, or grieves only briefly and then rallies to the resurrection. Paul says the opposite. He says we do not grieve as those who have no hope, which is not the same as we do not grieve. We grieve. We grieve hard. We just grieve toward something. The hope does not delete the grief. It gives the grief a direction.

When I teach my children about death, the most important thing I can give them is permission to be devastated. That the sadness is not a lack of faith, it is love with nowhere to go. That God is not offended by their tears, he collects them, the psalm says he keeps them in a bottle. A child who is allowed to grieve fully, in the presence of a parent who is also grieving and not pretending otherwise, learns something they cannot learn any other way, that the worst thing is real, that it can be survived, and that they are not alone in it. A child who is rushed past grief to the tidy comfort learns to distrust their own heart and to distrust the comfort.

There is a long-term cost to teaching a child that grief is faithlessness, and I have seen it in grown adults sitting in my office decades later. They lost a parent as a child, were told to be strong, were praised for how well they were handling it, and so they buried a grief that had nowhere to go, and it went underground, and it shaped them into adults who cannot feel loss, cannot cry, cannot let anything reach the buried place. They were faithful children. They were also, without knowing it, wounded ones, wounded not by the death but by the instruction to skip the grief. The resurrection does not require us to skip the grief. It promises to meet us on the far side of it, which is a different thing entirely.

## Telling the Truth About What We Do Not Know

Children ask the questions we have spent our whole adult lives avoiding. Where is Grandpa now. What is it like to be dead. Will it hurt. Will you die. Will I die. Why did God let it happen. And the temptation, always, is to answer with false certainty because false certainty feels like strength and the truth feels like abandoning them.

But false certainty is a debt that comes due. The child who is told exactly what heaven is like, in confident detail, will one day discover that we were guessing, and will wonder what else we were guessing about. The stronger answer, the one that actually holds up over a lifetime, is honest uncertainty inside a larger trust. I do not know exactly what it is like to be with God. The Bible gives us pictures, not a map. But I know God is good, I know Jesus went there first, and I know that wherever Grandpa is, he is not lost, because God does not lose people. I can say that and mean it. I cannot say Grandpa is watching over you from a cloud and mean it, so I do not say it.

> Children can carry the words I do not know if you carry them for them. It is not uncertainty that terrifies a child. It is uncertainty in the arms of a parent who is also terrified and pretending not to be.

This is the discipline that costs the most, because it requires the parent to tolerate their own not-knowing in front of a child who is begging for certainty. Every instinct in a parent's body wants to end the child's distress with a confident answer. But the confident answer we do not actually possess is a loan against a future the child will have to repay, and the honest answer, held steadily and warmly, is a gift they can keep. I do not know, but I trust him, and here is why. That sentence, from a parent who is clearly not panicking, does more for a child's faith than a dozen confident descriptions of the geography of heaven that the parent secretly made up.

## Let Them See You Grieve

My father died, and I made a decision, half-conscious, that my sons would see me cry. Not perform grief for their benefit, but not hide it either. Because I had been raised to believe that a man does not let his children see him break, and I have spent decades unlearning the damage of that belief, and I was not going to hand it down.

So they saw me cry at the funeral. They saw me quiet for weeks. They saw their father, the pastor, the one who is supposed to have answers, sit at the kitchen table and not have them. And I have come to believe that this was one of the most important things I ever gave them. Because now they know that grief does not end a man. That you can be shattered and still make breakfast. That faith is not the absence of tears, it is what you hold onto while you cry. If I had hidden my grief to protect them, I would have taught them that grief must be hidden, and I would have handed them, wrapped in love, the exact loneliness that nearly broke me at their age.

I grew up without a father, which means I never saw a man grieve, never saw a father cry, never had a model for how a man survives loss. I had to build that model from nothing, badly, in real time, in front of my own sons. And the thing I most wanted them to see was the thing I had never seen: a man who feels the full weight of a loss and does not pretend otherwise and does not let it destroy him and does not hide it from the people who love him. I do not know if I gave them that. I know I tried, at my father's funeral, with my own sons watching, to be the man I had needed and never had.

## The Long Conversation

Death is not a single conversation. It is a conversation that reopens at every age with new questions. The five-year-old asks if you will die. The nine-year-old asks what it means that a classmate's parent died. The thirteen-year-old asks whether heaven is even real. The seventeen-year-old, sitting up late after a friend's suicide, asks the question underneath all the others, whether anything means anything if it all ends. Each of these is the same child, coming back to the same edge, needing to know that the parent is still standing there, still honest, still unafraid to say I do not know and still sure that God is good.

What ruins this is a single early lie, delivered with confidence, that later gets exposed. The bathtub lie I told my son, not for a very long time, buddy, was a small one, and I have since gone back and told him a truer version, that I do not control when anyone dies, that I hope for a long life for him and cannot promise it, and that whatever happens, God does not lose the people he loves. He took it better than the lie deserved. Children usually do. They are stronger than our fear of their fear.

## What the Resurrection Actually Offers a Child

At the end, after all the honesty about grief and uncertainty, there is a thing we get to say to our children that no other worldview gets to say. Not that death is not sad. It is. Not that we know all the details of what comes after. We do not. But that death is not the last word. That the tomb was empty. That the God who wept at the grave of his friend is the same God who called him out of it. That the story does not end in the dark, even when the psalm does, even when the funeral does, even when the bathwater conversation does.

We do not give children this by skipping the grief. We give it to them by walking through the grief with them, all the way down, and then, from the bottom, pointing east. The hope is not a shortcut around the sorrow. It is a light that only makes sense once you have been in the dark long enough to need it. Our job is not to keep our children out of the dark. It is to be in there with them, holding their hand, telling the truth, and refusing to let go until the light comes up. It will come up. That is the one thing I am willing to promise them. It is the only thing I know for certain, and it is enough.

chapters.title: Digital Discipleship: Spiritual Formation in the Age of Algorithms
chapters.summary: The algorithm is not neutral. It is forming you into a particular kind of person, distracted, reactive, shallow, and perpetually outraged. The question is whether your faith is strong enough to resist it.
chapters.body:
In the year 2007, the average American spent approximately 2.7 hours per day consuming digital media. By 2023, that number had risen to over seven hours. In the space of sixteen years, the screens in our pockets have colonized more than a third of our waking hours. This is not a technological development. It is a spiritual one. Because whatever commands that much of your attention is, functionally, your liturgy. It is forming you. The only question is: into what?

The attention economy, the system in which technology companies compete for the limited resource of human attention in order to sell it to advertisers, is not merely an economic arrangement. It is, in the language of James K.A. Smith, a "liturgy of desire." It shapes what you want, how you see, and who you become. And it does so with a sophistication that would make the most accomplished spiritual director in Christian history weep with envy, because the algorithms that curate your digital experience know more about your desires, fears, and vulnerabilities than your pastor, your spouse, or your therapist.

The church has been remarkably slow to reckon with this. The dominant Christian responses to digital technology have been either uncritical adoption (churches migrating to Instagram, pastors building personal brands on Twitter, youth groups moving to TikTok) or blanket rejection (screen time is bad, social media is evil, delete your accounts). Neither response takes seriously the depth of the challenge. The attention economy is not a tool to be used or a temptation to be resisted. It is an environment that shapes the soul, and the Christian tradition has more resources for understanding that shaping than it has yet deployed. The question is not whether you will be formed by your digital environment. You will be. The question is whether you will be formed intentionally or by default, and the default, as we shall see, is not neutral.

## What the Attention Economy Does to Your Soul

The Desert Fathers and Mothers of the fourth century, Antony, Macarius, Evagrius, Syncletica, developed a sophisticated taxonomy of the spiritual dangers they called the *logismoi*, the patterns of thought that pull the soul away from God. Chief among them was *acedia*, a restless inability to stay present, a compulsive need for novelty and stimulation, a soul-deep resistance to the slow, patient work of prayer and self-examination. Evagrius called it "the noonday demon" because it struck hardest when the monk was supposed to be at prayer, filling the mind with thoughts of what else he could be doing, who else he could be talking to, what other place might be more interesting than this cell.

It is impossible to read the Desert Fathers' descriptions of acedia without recognizing the pathology they describe in our relationship with our phones. The compulsive checking. The inability to sit in silence. The restless scrolling through an infinite feed, not because any particular content satisfies but because the act of scrolling itself provides just enough dopamine to keep the hand moving. The Desert Fathers would have recognized our condition immediately. They would have called it what it is: a spiritual sickness, a soul habituated to distraction and thereby rendered incapable of the sustained attention that prayer, Scripture, and genuine human encounter require.

The neuroscience confirms what the monks intuited. Research from the laboratory of Adam Gazzaley at UC San Francisco has demonstrated that the constant task-switching demanded by digital media degrades the brain's capacity for sustained attention. The average attention span for a single task has decreased from twelve seconds in 2000 to approximately eight seconds, one second less than that attributed to a goldfish in the widely cited (though methodologically questionable) Microsoft study of 2015. Whether or not goldfish are the right comparison, the trend is not in dispute. We are becoming worse at paying attention, and the technologies we use are designed to make us worse.

The dopamine system is the mechanism. Every notification, every like, every new piece of content triggers a small release of dopamine, not the dopamine of satisfaction but the dopamine of anticipation, the neurochemical signature of "there might be something good here." This is the same system exploited by slot machines, and the parallel is not accidental. Former Facebook vice president Chamath Palihapitiya said in 2017: "The short-term, dopamine-driven feedback loops that we have created are destroying how society works." Tristan Harris, former Google design ethicist, has been even more explicit: "Your phone is a slot machine. Every time you check it, you are pulling the lever."

## The Performance of Faith Online

Social media has not merely distracted Christians from their faith. It has deformed the faith itself. The logic of social media, which rewards performance, controversy, brevity, and emotional intensity, is fundamentally incompatible with the logic of the gospel, which demands hiddenness, patience, nuance, and the willingness to say unpopular things without regard for the audience's reaction.

Jesus was explicit about this incompatibility, though he spoke about it in terms of the performative religion of his own day: "When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by others. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward in full. But when you pray, go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen" (Matthew 6:5-6). The principle is clear: authentic spiritual practice is incompatible with public performance. The moment you pray for an audience, you have stopped praying to God.

Social media is a street corner. Every post about your quiet time, every Instagram of your Bible and coffee, every tweet about what God is "teaching" you, every carefully curated image of your family devotions is a form of public prayer, prayer performed for the approval of the crowd. The likes and shares are the reward Jesus warned about. They are sufficient unto themselves and spiritually hollow.

The outrage cycles are equally deforming. The algorithm has learned that anger is the most engaging emotion, content that provokes outrage is shared more widely, generates more comments, and keeps users on the platform longer than any other type of content. Christians have been spectacularly susceptible to this dynamic. The culture war, which is, in many ways, a product of social media's incentive structures rather than a reflection of genuine cultural reality, has turned many Christians into people whose primary public witness is not love but anger. Not grace but condemnation. Not the patient, suffering, enemy-loving posture of Christ but the perpetually offended, constantly triggered posture of the algorithm's ideal user.

## Can You Be Formed Online?

The question of whether genuine spiritual formation can happen online is not a simple one, and the honest answer is: partially, but with severe limitations.

The COVID-19 pandemic forced a massive experiment in digital worship. When churches closed their buildings in March 2020, millions of Christians experienced worship exclusively through screens for months or, in some cases, years. The results were instructive. On the positive side, digital worship provided access to people who had been excluded from physical church: the homebound, the disabled, those living in areas without a church that fit their tradition. Sermon content, the intellectual and homiletical dimension of worship, translated reasonably well to digital formats.

But what did not translate was everything that makes worship more than a lecture. The embodied presence of other worshippers. The physical act of standing, sitting, kneeling, receiving bread and wine. The accidental conversations before and after the service that are often more pastorally significant than the sermon itself. The communal singing, which neuroscience has shown synchronizes heart rates and creates a physiological experience of unity that no video call can replicate. Digital worship, for all its accessibility, proved to be a reduced version of the real thing, serviceable in an emergency but insufficient as a long-term substitute.

Online Bible studies, devotional content, theological podcasts, and virtual spiritual direction can supplement spiritual formation. They cannot replace it. The reason is not merely practical but theological: Christianity is an incarnational faith. It insists that God did not merely transmit information to humanity but took on flesh and dwelt among us. The medium was the message. And a faith that is rooted in incarnation cannot be fully practiced in a disembodied medium.

## A Digital Rule of Life

The monastic tradition developed what it called a "rule of life", a set of practices, rhythms, and boundaries designed to shape the monk's day around the central priority of prayer and communion with God. The Rule of Saint Benedict, written in the sixth century, governed everything from meal times to sleeping arrangements to the hours of prayer. Its purpose was not legalistic control but the creation of an environment in which spiritual growth could happen, because Benedict understood that environment shapes character more reliably than willpower.

The contemporary Christian needs a digital rule of life for the same reason the sixth-century monk needed a monastic rule: because without intentional structure, the default environment will form you in ways you do not want to be formed. The algorithm's default formation is toward distraction, anxiety, comparison, outrage, and the endless consumption of novelty. A digital rule of life is a deliberate countermeasure.

The first element is temporal boundaries. Choose specific times of day when you will not use your phone, not as an exercise in willpower but as a structural protection of the activities that matter most. The first hour of the morning. The last hour before sleep. Mealtimes. The time you spend with your children. Worship. These are the hours when your attention is most valuable and most vulnerable, and ceding them to the algorithm is a choice with spiritual consequences whether you recognize it or not.

The second element is content curation. You are responsible for what you consume, and the algorithm will not curate your feed for your spiritual health. It will curate it for engagement, which means it will feed you whatever triggers the strongest emotional response, outrage, anxiety, envy, lust. Deliberately follow accounts and subscribe to content that forms you toward wisdom, compassion, and depth. Deliberately unfollow and mute content that forms you toward anger, comparison, and contempt. This is not avoidance. It is stewardship of the most limited resource you possess: your attention.

The third element is Sabbath from screens. The Jewish practice of Shabbat, one day in seven set apart from productive labor, is not merely a quaint religious tradition. It is an act of resistance against the totalizing claims of work, consumption, and productivity. A digital Sabbath, one day per week in which you do not check email, browse social media, or consume digital content, is the contemporary equivalent. It is the declaration that you are not available to the machine for twenty-four hours, that your attention belongs to God and to the people in front of you, and that the world will survive without your participation in the scroll.

The fourth element is silence. The Desert Fathers and Mothers understood that silence is not the absence of sound but the presence of attention. In silence, the soul hears what the noise has been drowning out, the voice of God, yes, but also the voice of your own deepest self, the self that has been buried under the avalanche of content, opinion, and stimulation. A daily practice of silence, even ten minutes, is profoundly countercultural. It is also profoundly necessary. Because a soul that cannot be silent cannot pray. And a soul that cannot pray is a soul that the algorithm has already claimed.

The screen is not your enemy. But it is not your friend either. It is a tool, and like every tool, it will be used by whoever holds it. The question is whether you are holding your phone or your phone is holding you. The answer, for most of us, is more uncomfortable than we would like to admit. And the first step toward freedom is the willingness to admit it.

chapters.title: Homeschool, Public, Private: The Education Decision
chapters.summary: The education decision has become a way for Christian parents to judge each other, and I have done my share of the judging, and I have been on the receiving end, and none of it was of God.
chapters.body:
The education decision has become a way for Christian parents to judge each other, and I have done my share of the judging, and I have been on the receiving end, and none of it was of God. There is a particular look a homeschool family gives a public school family, and a particular sigh a public school family gives a homeschool family, and a particular smugness the private school family manages to give both. And underneath the schooling debate, which pretends to be about pedagogy, is a war about who loves their children most and who is most faithful, and it is an ugly war, and Christians should be ashamed of how enthusiastically we wage it.

I have five sons, which over the years has meant navigating this decision more than once, in different seasons, with different children, and I want to say the thing that the loud voices in each camp do not want said. There is no universally right answer. There is no single faithful choice. The parents who tell you otherwise, in any direction, are selling you their anxiety dressed as conviction, and I have bought it and sold it both.

## The False Certainty in Every Camp

Each schooling tribe has its gospel, and each gospel is a half-truth inflated into a whole one. The homeschool gospel says that only by removing your children from the world's system can you protect their faith and shape their character, and that to hand them to the state for eight hours a day is to hand them to the enemy. The private Christian school gospel says that you need trained teachers and a Christian environment and academic rigor that homeschooling cannot match and public schools have abandoned. The public school gospel says that faith grows strong in the real world, that salt and light belong in the culture not sequestered from it, and that the other two options are fear dressed as faithfulness.

> Every camp has taken a genuine good and turned it into a law, and then used the law to condemn the parents in the other camps. The homeschooler's protection, the private schooler's rigor, the public schooler's engagement, each of them is a real good, and none of them is a command from God.

Notice that each gospel contains real truth. Homeschooling does allow unmatched shaping of a child's environment. Christian schools do offer a formative community and can provide excellent education. Public schools do put children in the actual world where actual faith has to be lived. The error is never in the truth each camp holds. The error is in the absolutizing, in taking your family's wise choice for your children and universalizing it into the faithful choice for all children, and then judging the parents who chose differently as either fearful or negligent. That judgment is the sin, and it lives in all three houses.

And each camp has its horror stories, which it deploys to frighten the others. The homeschoolers have the story of the sheltered kid who left home unprepared and lost their faith at the first party. The private schoolers have the story of the public school child corrupted by the culture. The public schoolers have the story of the homeschooled child who could not function socially. Every one of these stories is real. And every one of them is a single data point weaponized into a universal law, which is precisely how fear masquerades as wisdom. The child who fell apart did not fall apart because of the schooling choice. They fell apart for reasons that ran deeper than any building, and the camp that tells the story has simply pinned a complicated tragedy on the choice they already disapproved of.

## Why the Bible Does Not Settle This

Christians who want a proof text for their schooling choice go hunting through Scripture and come back with ammunition, and the ammunition is always thinner than they claim. Yes, Deuteronomy commands parents to teach their children, and homeschoolers wield this, but it commands parents to teach diligently at all times, which no schooling arrangement fulfills or prevents. Yes, Jesus prayed that his followers would be in the world but not of it, and public schoolers wield this, but it does not prescribe a specific institution. Yes, we are told bad company corrupts good character, and private schoolers wield this, but bad company exists in every school including the Christian ones.

The reason the Bible does not settle the schooling question is that the Bible is not about schooling. It is about the formation of the whole person by the whole family in the whole life of faith, and that formation can happen, or fail to happen, in any educational setting. The determining factor in whether a child's faith survives is not the building they sit in for six hours a day. It is the household they come home to, the parents they watch, the God they see modeled or not modeled at the dinner table. The schooling debate assigns to the school a formative power that actually belongs, overwhelmingly, to the home. We are arguing about the wrong variable.

## What Actually Shapes a Child

The research and the pastoral experience agree, and they agree against the loudest voices in every camp. The single strongest predictor of a child's faith and character is not their school. It is their parents, their home, the authenticity of the faith they witness up close over years. A child in a public school with parents whose faith is real and lived and honest is far more spiritually protected than a child in a Christian school with parents whose faith is a performance. The school is a secondary variable. The home is the primary one. And the schooling debate almost entirely ignores this, because it is more comfortable to obsess over the choice of institution than to face the harder question of whether our own faith at home is real.

> We fight about schools because it is easier than facing the truth that our children are formed mostly by us. The building is a variable we can control by choosing. The kind of parent we are is a variable we would have to change, and changing is harder than choosing.

This reframes the whole decision. Instead of asking which school will save my child, which no school will do, the question becomes which arrangement best fits this particular child, this particular family, in this particular season, given our resources, our children's temperaments, our local options, and our capacity. That is a wisdom question, not a law question. It will have different answers for different families and even for different children in the same family, which is exactly what parents of many children discover and what the ideologues cannot accept.

## Different Children, Different Answers

One of the things having several children taught me is that the right schooling choice can differ from child to child, which detonates the whole premise that there is one faithful answer. A child who is thriving and anchored might flourish in a public school and be a genuine light there. A child who is struggling, or particularly vulnerable in some way, might need the smaller and more protected environment of homeschooling for a season. A child with specific gifts might be best served by a particular school that can develop them. The wise parent fits the schooling to the child, not the child to an ideology.

This is impossible for the ideologue to hear, because the ideologue has decided in advance, on principle, and applies the principle to every child regardless of the child. But children are not interchangeable, and a decision that serves one child can genuinely harm another. Loving your children well sometimes means schooling them differently, which will horrify your tribe and confuse your friends and require you to explain, repeatedly, that you are not being inconsistent, you are being attentive. The consistency the ideologues demand is a consistency to the ideology, not to the actual children, and the actual children are what we are supposed to be raising.

## The Cost of the War

Consider what the schooling war costs the church. It divides Christian parents into hostile camps who cannot fellowship without an undercurrent of judgment. It makes the education decision, which should be a matter of prayerful family wisdom, into a public loyalty test. It causes parents to choose out of fear of judgment rather than out of genuine discernment about their own child. And it teaches our watching children that Christians are people who judge each other over secondary matters, which may do more damage to their faith than any school ever could.

I have felt the pull to defend my family's choices against the implied criticism of parents who chose differently, and every time I have given in to that pull I have contributed to the war. The homeschool family does not need my defensiveness and the public school family does not need my superiority and none of us needs the constant low-grade judgment we pour on each other in the name of caring most about our children. It is possible, and it should be normal, for a homeschool family and a public school family and a private school family to sit at the same table, break the same bread, and honor each other's discernment without a single judgment passing between them. That it is not normal is an indictment of us.

The deeper reason we fight so hard about schooling is that the choice has become a marker of identity, a way of signaling which kind of Christian family we are, which tribe we belong to, which values we hold. The homeschool choice, the private school choice, the public school choice, each carries a whole cluster of cultural and theological associations, and to choose is to declare an allegiance, and to encounter a family that chose differently is to encounter a rival allegiance, and so the schooling conversation becomes a proxy war for a much larger set of anxieties about who we are and whether we are doing this Christian life correctly. This is why the debate carries so much more heat than the stakes actually warrant, why parents who agree about the gospel and the creed and the cross can find themselves genuinely estranged over a decision about buildings. The building became a badge. And when a decision becomes a badge, we stop asking what serves this particular child and start asking what proves we are the right kind of parent, which is exactly the wrong question, and it is a question the enemy of our souls is delighted to keep us arguing about, because every hour we spend judging each other's schools is an hour we are not spending being the parents our children actually need.

## The Freedom in This

Here is the grace at the end of the schooling debate. You are free. Genuinely free. God has not hidden a single correct schooling choice in Scripture that you must divine or fail your children. He has given you your children, your circumstances, your local options, and his Spirit, and he has asked you to make a wise and prayerful decision that fits your family, and then to trust him with the outcome, and then, crucially, to make that decision again as circumstances change, without treating your previous decision or anyone else's as a law.

This freedom is harder to receive than a rule would be, which is why so many parents secretly want the rule. A rule tells you exactly what to do and relieves you of the burden of discernment and the risk of being wrong. Freedom hands the burden back. It says, I have given you wisdom and my Spirit and the actual knowledge of your actual child, and I am trusting you to decide, and to decide again as things change. That is a heavier thing to carry than a commandment, because you cannot outsource the responsibility to a formula, and you cannot escape the possibility that you will choose imperfectly. But it is also the only honest way to raise the child you actually have, rather than the abstract child the ideologies imagine. God did not give you a policy. He gave you a person, this specific son or daughter with this specific temperament and these specific needs, and he asked you to love them wisely, which sometimes means one school and sometimes means another, and always means paying more attention to the child in front of you than to the tribe watching over your shoulder.

What matters is not the building. What matters is the home you send them out from and welcome them back to, the faith they see in you when no one is teaching, the God who is real in your house or is not. Get that right, and your children have a fighting chance in any school. Get that wrong, and no school will save them. So make the schooling decision with wisdom and hold it with humility, and pour your real energy into the thing that actually forms your children, which is you, and which no institution can outsource or replace. The education decision matters less than we fight about it, and the home matters more than we admit, and the judgment we heap on each other over the first is a way of avoiding the second. Stop fighting the war. Go home and be the parent your child is actually watching. That is the decision that decides everything.

chapters.title: Parenting a Child with Special Needs
chapters.summary: The world measures children by what they achieve. A child with special needs exposes that measure as a lie, and reveals a gospel that never valued us for our productivity at all.
chapters.body:
I want to write about something I have witnessed closely in ministry but have not lived from the inside in the way that parents of children with special needs have lived it. So I write with a particular humility here, aware that there are things about this road that only those who walk it can fully know. But I have sat with enough of these families, in the hospital rooms and the therapy waiting areas and the quiet living rooms after the diagnosis, to have learned some things worth saying, and to have had my own theology broken open and rebuilt by what they taught me.

What I have learned, above all, is that a child with special needs exposes a lie that most of us live inside without ever noticing it. The lie is that human worth is tied to human achievement, that we matter because of what we can do, produce, accomplish, contribute. Our whole civilization is built on this lie, and most of our churches, whatever they say on Sunday, are built on it too. And a child who will never achieve by those measures stands as a living refutation of the whole system, and reveals a gospel that never valued any of us for our productivity in the first place.

## The grief no one lets you name

Before anything else, there is grief, and it is a grief the world does not know how to let you have. When a child is born with, or later diagnosed with, a significant disability, a parent grieves. Not the child, who is loved fiercely and completely, but the loss of the imagined future, the expectations quietly assembled during the pregnancy, the life the parent had pictured that will now not be. This grief is real and it is legitimate, and yet parents are often made to feel they cannot voice it, because to grieve the imagined child seems like a rejection of the actual child.

It is not. A parent can love their child completely and still grieve the future they thought they would have. The two are not in conflict. The grief must be allowed to breathe, to be named, to be brought before God honestly, because grief that is suppressed does not disappear. It goes underground and poisons. The parents I have watched flourish in this calling are the ones who were permitted, by their community and by their own honesty, to grieve fully, and then to move through the grief into a love that was not diminished by having grieved. The church that tells such parents they should feel only blessing, only joy, only gratitude, robs them of the honesty their souls require.

> You can love your child with your whole heart and still grieve the future you imagined. Do not let anyone shame you out of the grief. Grief honored becomes love deepened. Grief denied becomes love poisoned.

The grief does not resolve once and disappear. It returns, often, at the thresholds, at the birthday parties for other children, at the milestones that will not come, at the moment a younger sibling passes the older child in some capacity the older child will never reach. This recurring grief is not a failure of acceptance or a lack of faith. It is the ongoing cost of loving deeply in a world that is not yet what it will be, and it deserves to be met with tenderness, not with a demand that the parent should be over it by now.

## The idol of the productive life

Our society has made an idol of productivity, and the idol demands human sacrifice. We measure a person's worth by their output, their achievement, their contribution to the economy and the accumulation of accomplishments. And this idol reaches into places we do not notice, including the way we love our children, the pride we take in their achievements, the quiet way we treat their accomplishments as a reflection of our own worth as parents.

A child with profound special needs cannot participate in this economy of worth, and their existence therefore functions as a prophetic word against it. Here is a human being, fully and completely a person, made in the image of God, precious beyond measure, who will never produce, achieve, or contribute in the ways the idol demands. And their preciousness is not one bit diminished by that fact. If we can see this clearly, we discover that the idol was always a lie, that human worth was never about productivity, that every one of us was loved by God before we produced anything and would be loved by God if we produced nothing at all.

> A child who will never achieve by the world's measures is a prophet against the world's measures. Their worth, undiminished by their limitations, exposes the lie that any of our worth was ever about achievement.

Jean Vanier, who gave his life to communities where those with profound intellectual disabilities lived alongside those without, insisted that such persons were not merely recipients of care but bearers of a gift, that they revealed to the rest of us the poverty of our own hearts and the truth of our own dependence. Whatever we make of the failures that later came to light in his own life, the truth he pointed to remains, and it is a truth the church has been slow to receive. The person the world overlooks is often the one placed among us to heal us of the very blindness that makes us overlook them.

## What the image of God actually means

We say that human beings are made in the image of God, but we often smuggle into that phrase an assumption that the image consists in our capacities, our reason, our will, our ability to do things. And if the image of God were located in our capacities, then a person with diminished capacities would bear a diminished image, which is a monstrous conclusion that the Scripture nowhere supports.

The image of God is not a set of abilities we possess. It is a status we are given, a dignity conferred by the Creator, a belonging that does not depend on what we can do. The theologian who taught me this most clearly insisted that the image is about being addressed by God, being in relationship, being held in the divine regard, and none of that depends on cognitive capacity or physical ability. A child who cannot speak, cannot reason as others reason, cannot care for themselves, bears the full and undiminished image of God, and is fully and completely a person whom God addresses and holds and loves. To see this is to have your entire theology of the human person corrected by a child the world would overlook.

## The gift hidden in the dependence

There is a gift buried in the profound dependence of a child with severe special needs, though it is a gift wrapped in exhaustion and hard to receive. The gift is a truth about all of us that we spend our lives denying. We are all dependent. We all began in total helplessness and will very likely end there, and in between we sustain the illusion of self-sufficiency that our culture prizes. The child who never outgrows dependence holds up a mirror to the human condition that the rest of us work hard to avoid.

And the dependence, rightly seen, is not a defect but a revelation. It reveals that we were made for relationship, for receiving, for being held, and that the myth of the independent self is exactly that, a myth. The parent who cares for a fully dependent child is living inside a truth about love that the rest of us only glimpse, the truth that love is not a transaction between equals who exchange value, but a giving that asks nothing in return, that finds its meaning in the giving itself. This is, not incidentally, exactly how God loves us. We are all far more dependent on God than we admit, and the child who cannot pretend otherwise teaches the rest of us what we are.

There is a further truth hidden here that our achievement-obsessed culture cannot easily see. The child who receives and cannot repay is not the diminished partner in the relationship of love. In some ways they are the one who gives the greater gift, because they give the parent the chance to love without the corrupting motive of return, to love in the purest form love can take, the form that expects nothing back. We are so trained to think of the caregiver as the giver and the cared-for as the receiver that we miss the reciprocity that runs the other way. The child gives the parent an occasion to become a certain kind of person, a person capable of a love the world barely believes in, a love that most of us, tangled as we are in transactions, never fully learn. The one the world would call a burden is, in the deep economy of the soul, a giver of the rarest gift, the gift of an object for love that asks for nothing in return.

## The siblings who also carry it

There is a dimension of this road that is easy to overlook, and it is the experience of the other children in the family, the siblings of the child with special needs. They grow up in a home where an enormous share of the family's time, energy, and attention is necessarily directed toward one child, and they learn, often, to ask for little, to make themselves easy, to carry needs of their own that go unspoken because they can see that their parents are already stretched to the breaking point.

These siblings often become remarkable people, marked by a compassion and a maturity beyond their years. But they also carry a hidden weight, and they need to be seen in it. They need a parent who notices that they too are children with needs, who finds moments to give them undivided attention, who does not allow their goodness and their ease to become an excuse for their neglect. And they need permission to feel the complicated things they feel, the love for their sibling tangled up with resentment, guilt, embarrassment, and grief, without being shamed for the feelings that are the honest fruit of a hard situation. A family raising a child with special needs is raising all its children in the shadow of that reality, and the ones without the diagnosis are shaped by it just as deeply, and deserve to be seen just as clearly.

## The community that must show up

Here again the church is tested and often found wanting. Families raising children with special needs frequently find themselves isolated, exhausted, and quietly excluded from the life of a church that was not built with their child in mind. The service that cannot accommodate a child who makes noise. The children's ministry with no place for a child who does not fit the standard program. The well-meaning members who do not know what to say and so say nothing, and by their silence communicate that this family is a burden rather than a gift.

A church that believes what it says about the image of God will move heaven and earth to include these families, will build the ramps and train the volunteers and make the space, will treat the child with special needs not as a challenge to be accommodated but as a member of the body whose presence blesses the whole. The measure of a church's theology is not what it says about human dignity in the abstract but how it treats the child who cannot contribute in the currency the world values. If we cannot make room for that child, we have not understood the gospel we claim to preach.

## The love that reveals God

I have watched parents of children with special needs love in a way that has taught me more about the love of God than most sermons I have heard, including my own. Because it is a love that expects nothing back, that gives and gives to a child who may never say thank you, may never understand the sacrifice, may never be able to reciprocate. And in that one-directional, cost-absorbing, expecting-nothing love, I have seen the clearest earthly picture of how God loves us.

God's love for us is not a response to our achievements or a reward for our contribution. It is a love that gives to those who can give nothing back, that pours out on the helpless and the dependent, that asks nothing and offers everything. The parent who loves a profoundly disabled child is not merely enduring a hardship. They are participating in the very heart of God, living out the divine love in the flesh, teaching the watching world what love actually is when it is stripped of transaction and reduced to its essence. If you are that parent, know this: you are not merely surviving. You are revealing God. And the child you love, whom the world would overlook, is one of the clearest windows into the kingdom that I know.

chapters.title: Parenting in the Digital Age: Screens, Souls, and Boundaries
chapters.summary: The screen is not neutral. It is designed to capture what we were meant to give to God and each other. Parenting through it requires more than filters. It requires formation.
chapters.body:
I raised my older sons before the smartphone and my younger sons after it, and the difference is one of the starkest natural experiments I have ever lived inside. The world my oldest navigated as a teenager and the world my youngest navigates are not the same world, and anyone who tells you the difference is merely a matter of new tools has not paid attention. The screen did not just give our children new things to do. It rewired the environment in which their souls are being formed.

I want to resist two easy responses here, because both let us off the hook. One is the panic that treats every screen as poison and every parent who allows one as negligent. The other is the shrug that treats the technology as neutral, just a tool, no different in kind from a book or a telephone. Neither is honest. The screen is not neutral, but the answer is not panic. The answer is formation, and formation is much harder than either fear or indifference.

## The screen is designed, and not for your child's good

Let us begin with what we would rather not say. The devices in our children's hands were designed by some of the most brilliant minds of our time, funded by some of the largest fortunes ever assembled, for a single purpose: to capture and hold human attention. Not to inform. Not to connect. To capture. The business model depends on it. Every feature that keeps a child scrolling was engineered to keep them scrolling, and the engineers know exactly what they are doing, because they measure it.

This matters theologically, because attention is not a trivial thing. Attention is close to the center of the spiritual life. What we attend to shapes what we love, and what we love shapes who we become. Simone Weil said that attention, absolute unmixed attention, is prayer. And here is a machine, in your child's hand, engineered by an industry to fragment attention into ten-second pieces and sell those pieces to advertisers. We are not fighting a neutral tool. We are fighting a deliberate assault on the very faculty by which a soul learns to love God and neighbor.

> The screen is not competing with your child's boredom. It is competing with their capacity for attention, and attention is the faculty by which they will one day learn to pray, to love, and to be present. This is a battle for something sacred.

The social psychologist Jonathan Haidt has documented the sharp inflection that arrived when the smartphone and the social platform reached the hands of adolescents, and the timing of the rise in anxiety, depression, and self-harm that followed it. Correlation is not the whole story, and honest people can argue about mechanisms. But the pattern is stark enough that no thoughtful parent can dismiss it, and it lines up with what any of us can observe in our own homes. Something has changed in the inner lives of the young, and the device in their pocket is somewhere near the center of it.

## Filters are not formation

The first instinct of the anxious Christian parent is technical. Install the filter. Set the controls. Monitor the usage. And there is a place for these things, especially with younger children, because you do not hand a child a loaded environment and call it freedom. But filters address the wrong problem. Filters keep bad content out. They do nothing to form the soul that will one day, inevitably, encounter the bad content without a filter.

The goal is not a child who cannot access harm because you blocked it. The goal is a child who has been formed into a person who can navigate a world full of harm with wisdom and self-possession. And that formation does not come from software. It comes from the slow, relational work of teaching a child to understand what the screen is doing to them, to notice the pull, to develop the internal muscles of restraint that no external filter can substitute for. A child raised only on filters arrives at eighteen with no filter and no internal formation, which is the worst of both worlds.

This is not an argument against filters. It is an argument against relying on them. The filter buys time, and time is valuable, because it delays exposure until a child is more capable of handling it. But the time must be used, not merely bought. If the years behind the filter are not spent forming a child's judgment, their appetites, their capacity for self-restraint, then the filter has only postponed the reckoning, and the reckoning will arrive against a soul no more prepared for it than before.

## What the screen displaces

The real cost of the screen is often not what it shows but what it displaces. Every hour on the device is an hour not spent in the activities that form a healthy soul. Boredom, which is the seedbed of imagination, is now instantly abolished at the first flicker of discomfort. Solitude, which is where a person learns to be at peace with their own company and, eventually, with God, is now impossible, because the device ensures no one is ever alone with their thoughts.

Face-to-face relationship, with all its friction and its irreplaceable richness, is thinned out and replaced by mediated connection that feels like relationship but delivers a fraction of its nourishment. And the developing brain, which needs deep rest, is instead kept in a state of low-grade stimulation late into the night. What the screen displaces is often more damaging than what it delivers. A childhood without boredom, without solitude, without unhurried presence, is a childhood missing the very conditions in which depth grows.

> Ask not only what your child is consuming on the screen. Ask what the screen is preventing them from ever experiencing. The absence of boredom is not a gift. It is the theft of imagination.

Boredom is not the enemy we have made it out to be. Boredom is the doorway to imagination, to creativity, to the interior life. A child who is never bored never learns to generate their own inner world, never discovers that the most interesting thing available is not on a screen but inside their own restless, God-given mind. When we rush to eliminate every moment of boredom with a device, we are not being kind. We are amputating a faculty, and the child will grow up unable to be alone with themselves, terrified of the silence in which God is most often found.

## The parent in the mirror

Here is where I must implicate myself, and where most of the parenting advice on this subject goes quiet, because it is more comfortable to talk about the children's screens than our own. My children learned their relationship with the screen partly by watching mine. When I checked my phone at dinner, I taught them that the meal was less important than whatever was in my hand. When I responded to a text mid-conversation with my son, I taught him that his father's attention was always provisional, always interruptible, always available to be claimed by someone else.

I cannot count the times a son was telling me something and I was half-present, my eyes drifting to the screen, my thumb already scrolling. I told myself I was listening. I was not. And a child knows the difference between a parent who is present and a parent who is performing presence while their attention is elsewhere. Before I lecture my children about their screen habits, I have to reckon with the fact that I formed those habits, in part, by the example of my own divided attention. The hypocrisy is not lost on them, and it should not be lost on us.

## Boundaries as gifts, not punishments

When boundaries do come, and they must, the framing matters enormously. A boundary presented as a punishment, as distrust, as the parent asserting control, invites resistance and teaches the child that the screen is a prize being withheld. A boundary presented as a gift, as a protection of something valuable, as the family together choosing to guard its attention and its presence, invites participation.

The most effective boundaries are the ones the whole family keeps together. The phones that sleep outside the bedroom, all of them, the parents' included. The dinner table where no one, adult or child, brings a device. The stretch of Sabbath where the whole household unplugs together. These are not rules imposed from above. They are practices the family embraces together, and they form everyone, including the parents who most need forming. A child who watches their father put his own phone away for the sake of presence learns something no lecture could teach.

## Forming the appetite, not just restricting the intake

Ultimately, parenting in the digital age is about forming an appetite, not just restricting an intake. A child who is only restricted, only blocked, only told no, develops a hunger for the forbidden thing and a plan to access it the moment they are free. A child whose appetites are being formed toward better things, who has tasted the deep satisfaction of a long book, an unhurried conversation, a project made with their hands, a walk with nowhere to be, is developing an internal compass that will serve them when the external controls fall away.

This is the harder work, and the slower work, and the work that no app can do for you. It means providing the alternatives, the analog richness, the family culture in which the screen is not the default but one option among many that are actually more compelling. It means being present enough, unhurried enough, un-distracted enough yourself, that your presence is more attractive than the device. That last one indicts me most of all, because a child will not choose the parent over the screen if the parent is always half inside a screen of their own.

## The comparison machine and the young soul

There is a particular harm the screen does to the adolescent soul that deserves naming on its own, because it is more insidious than the obvious dangers we warn about. The platforms our children inhabit are comparison machines. They present, endlessly, a curated highlight reel of everyone else's life, against which the ordinary reality of the child's own life cannot help but look impoverished. A young person scrolling through the polished, filtered, carefully staged images of their peers is being fed, hour after hour, the lie that everyone else is happier, more beautiful, more included, more successful than they are.

This is spiritual poison of a specific kind. Envy has always been a threat to the soul, but never before has a machine been engineered to manufacture envy at industrial scale and deliver it directly into the mind of a developing child. The old wisdom that we should not compare ourselves to others was hard enough to follow when comparison meant the few neighbors we could see. Now the comparison is with a curated infinity, an endless feed of everyone's best moment, and the young soul measures its ordinary Tuesday against a thousand highlight reels and concludes that it is failing. To form a child who can resist this is to form a child who knows their worth does not come from the feed, who can look away, who can be content with an unremarkable life that is nonetheless their own and nonetheless loved by God.

There is another layer to this that cuts even deeper, and it is the way the platforms teach a young person to perform their own life rather than to live it. When every experience is potential content, when the value of a moment is measured by how it will look to an audience, the child learns to stand outside their own life, curating it, packaging it, watching themselves be watched. This is a kind of exile from the self, a loss of the capacity to simply be present in an experience without the running commentary of how it will play. A young person formed this way loses something precious, the ability to have an experience that belongs only to them, unphotographed, unposted, unwitnessed by anyone but God. To give your child moments that are not content, experiences that exist only for their own sake, is to give them back a piece of their own soul that the platforms are quietly stealing. The unposted moment, the memory kept private, the joy that no one else sees, is a form of wealth the comparison machine cannot touch.

The digital age is not going away, and I am not calling you to pretend it is. I am calling you to something more demanding than filters and more honest than panic. I am calling you to form your children, and yourself, into people whose attention is not for sale, whose presence is not fragmented, whose souls are not colonized by an industry that profits from their distraction. That formation begins with the phone in your own hand. Put it down. Look at your child. Be there. The most radical thing you can do in the digital age is to give your child your undivided attention, because you will be teaching them, by doing it, what they are worth.

chapters.title: Parenting Through Divorce
chapters.summary: You will want to explain to your children why it was the other parent's fault. Do not. That impulse feels like justice. It is a knife you are handing your child.
chapters.body:
You will want to explain to your children why it was the other parent's fault. Do not. That impulse feels like justice, feels like protecting them from a distorted version of events, feels like the truth they deserve. It is a knife, and you are handing it to your child to carry, and it will cut them for the rest of their lives, not the parent you aimed it at.

I am a pastor. I believe marriage is meant to last, and I do not write this to make divorce comfortable. I write it because divorce happens, it happens in the church, it happens to people who fought for their marriages and to people who did not, and when it happens there are children in the house, and those children did not choose any of it, and how the parents behave in the wreckage will shape those children more than the divorce itself. The divorce is a wound. The way you handle it is either a bandage or salt.

## The Thing Children Actually Fear

Ask children of divorce what they were most afraid of, and it is almost never the logistics. It is the fear that it was their fault, and the fear that a parent who left the marriage might leave them too. Children are natural egocentrists, not out of selfishness but out of developmental necessity, and a young child genuinely believes the world revolves around them, which means when the world breaks, they assume they broke it. If I had been better, if I had not fought with my brother, if I had been easier, they would have stayed together.

> The child is not asking whose fault the divorce was. The child is asking whether the divorce was their fault. And every argument you win in front of them about the other parent confirms their worst fear, that the family is a war and they are somewhere near the cause.

You have to say it, out loud, more than once, in words a child can hold. This is not your fault. Nothing you did caused this and nothing you could have done would have prevented it.
