This is between the adults, and both of us still love you, and that is never going to change. You will feel like you are stating the obvious. You are not. The child does not know it. The child needs to hear it from both parents, repeatedly, over years, because the fear is not defeated in one conversation. It comes back at every developmental stage in a new disguise.

The second fear, that a parent who left the marriage might leave the child, is subtler and just as real. A child watches one parent walk away from a relationship they thought was permanent, and the child does the math. If that bond could break, what about mine. This is why divorced parents have to be almost obsessively reliable about the small things, the pickups, the promises, the phone calls, the being where you said you would be when you said you would be there. Every kept promise is evidence against the fear. Every broken one confirms it. The child is running an experiment, mostly unconsciously, on whether the adults in their life can be counted on, and the divorce has already returned one frightening result. Your reliability is how you argue with it.

## Do Not Make Them a Messenger

The single most damaging habit in a divorce is turning the child into a courier. Tell your father he still owes for the field trip. Ask your mother why she was late again. Every message you send through the child forces the child to carry your conflict on their small back, across the demilitarized zone, into the other parent's house, where they will absorb the return fire. You have made your child a diplomat in a war they did not start and cannot end.

Children are not messengers. They are not spies, either, though divorced parents interrogate them constantly, what did your mother say, is there a new man there, how much did that cost, framed as concern, functioning as reconnaissance. The child learns to manage information between two hostile powers, to say different things in different houses, to survive by becoming a small deceiver. This is corrosive to the soul of a child. The adults have to communicate with each other, directly, even when it is excruciating, so that the child can just be a child in both houses instead of a courier in neither.

I know how hard the direct communication is, because the whole reason you divorced is often that direct communication became unbearable. But the alternative, routing your conflict through a child, does not spare the child the conflict. It embeds them in it. If you cannot talk to your former spouse without it becoming a fight, then use writing, use a scheduling app, use a mediator, use anything that is not your nine-year-old. The child is not a neutral channel. The child loves both of you, which means every message they carry costs them something in loyalty and every hostility they witness lands on a heart that is already divided in half.

## Do Not Recruit Them

There is a deeper betrayal than using a child as a messenger, and it is using a child as a confidant. The lonely, wounded parent who, out of genuine pain, begins to lean on the child emotionally, to share adult grievances, to make the child their support system, their ally, their friend. It feels like closeness. The child even seems to want it, seems mature enough for it, rises to it. It is one of the most damaging things a parent can do.

> When you make your child your emotional support, you have not gained an ally. You have lost a child. You have handed them a weight they were never built to carry, and they will carry it, because they love you, and it will bend them.

The child who becomes the parent's confidant loses their childhood. They become anxiously attuned to the adult's emotional state, responsible for a grief they cannot fix, and torn in half when the confided-in grievance is about the other parent they also love. They are being asked to take a side in the destruction of their own family. Some of them do take a side, and it looks like loyalty, and it is really a child being conscripted. Your grief is real and it deserves support. It deserves support from other adults. Your child is not a peer, no matter how mature they seem, and treating them as one steals something from them they do not get back.

This is hardest for the parent who is genuinely alone, whose marriage ended and whose support system thinned out at the same time, and whose most available, most sympathetic listener is the child sitting across the table. I understand the pull. But the pull has to be resisted, precisely because it is so strong and the child is so willing. A twelve-year-old who has become their mother's best friend is not being honored by the closeness. They are being robbed of the freedom to be twelve, to have their own problems be the big problems, to lean on the adult instead of propping the adult up. Find adult support, however hard that is to find, so that your child gets to keep being your child.

## Two Houses, One Childhood

The practical work of parenting through divorce is the work of protecting the child's world from becoming a battlefield of contrasts. Two households, run by two hurt people, will differ. But the more the child experiences the two houses as opposed camps with opposed values, the more the child has to fracture themselves to belong in both. Consistency between houses, on the things that matter, bedtimes, expectations, the basic sense of what is right, is a gift to the child's coherence. You are not doing it for your ex. You are doing it so your child does not have to be two different people.

This requires something almost impossible, a working relationship with the person who broke your heart. Not friendship. Not forgiveness on any timeline that can be rushed. A working relationship, businesslike, focused entirely on the child, in which you can sit at the same graduation and the same wedding decades later without the child having to manage your feelings. The parents who achieve this, and some do, give their children something worth more than the intact marriage would have given a different family, proof that love for a child can outlast the love between the adults.

## Your Anger Is Real, and It Is Not the Child's to Hold

None of this means your anger is wrong. If you were betrayed, abandoned, or wounded, the anger is righteous and it deserves a place. It deserves a therapist, a pastor, a friend, a journal, the psalms of lament that were written by people who wanted God to break the teeth of their enemies. God can hold your rage. Your congregation can hold your grief. What cannot hold it, what must not be asked to hold it, is a nine-year-old who loves both of the people you are enraged at each other about.

I have sat with divorced parents who were doing everything right in every visible way and were still leaking their bitterness into the child through a thousand small tells, the tone when the other parent's name comes up, the tightness at drop-off, the sigh. Children read these fluently. The work is not to feel nothing. That is impossible. The work is to find adult places for the adult feelings so that the child gets a parent instead of a co-belligerent.

There is a particular temptation that deserves naming, because it is so easy to justify. It is the temptation to let the child see just a little of the truth about the other parent, to plant one small correction, to make sure the child knows, quietly, who was really at fault. It never feels like weaponizing the child. It feels like honesty, like fairness, like refusing to let a lie stand. But the child does not experience it as fairness. The child experiences it as being asked to hold their parent in contempt, and every such request, however small, however justified, tears at the child's own sense of self, because the child is made of both of you. To ask a child to despise one parent is to ask them to despise half of themselves. Whatever the other parent did, and it may have been genuinely terrible, the child's need to love both of you intact is more important than your need to be proven right, and the parent who grasps this, and holds their tongue at the cost of never getting the vindication they crave, is giving the child something worth more than the truth about who broke the marriage.

## What Grace Looks Like in the Wreckage

I said I am a pastor and I believe marriage is meant to last. I also believe in grace, and grace is not a doctrine that lives in the abstract, it is a way of behaving toward people who have hurt you. The parent who, in the wreckage of a divorce, refuses to weaponize the children, who honors the other parent in front of them even while grieving privately, who absorbs the messenger role instead of assigning it, who finds adult support instead of conscripting the child, is doing something profoundly Christlike. They are absorbing cost so that someone smaller does not have to. That is the shape of the cross, transposed into custody arrangements and drop-off schedules.

None of this is possible in your own strength, and I will not pretend it is. To honor the person who betrayed you, to hold your tongue when you could win the child to your side, to absorb the messenger role and the loneliness and the rage without leaking any of it onto a child, is genuinely beyond the natural capacity of a wounded human heart. It requires grace poured into you before you can pour it out, the grace of a God who himself absorbed betrayal and did not retaliate, who was wronged past all measure and answered with forgiveness. You will not manufacture this behavior by trying harder. You will only find it by going to the God who did it first and asking him to do it in you, over and over, on the hard mornings, at the drop-offs, in the moments when everything in you wants to make the child understand who the real villain was. The grace you extend to your former spouse for the sake of your children is not something you generate. It is something you receive and pass through, and the passing through is itself the healing, both for you and for the children who are watching.

Your children are watching how you treat the person who hurt you most. They will learn, from that, more about the gospel than from every sermon they hear, because they will see whether grace is real or only spoken. The divorce is not the last word over your children. The way you carry them through it can be a testimony louder than the marriage would ever have been. Not because the divorce was good. It was not. But because grace does its best work exactly where things have broken, and your children are old enough to see, in you, whether you believe that or only preach it. Show them. It is the most important sermon you will ever give, and you will give it without words, in the years when it costs the most.

chapters.title: Raising Daughters in a World That Objectifies Them
chapters.summary: I have five sons and no daughters, which means I write this as an outsider to the specific war being waged on the girls in your house. But I have watched the war, and I know the lie at the center of it.
chapters.body:
I have five sons and no daughters. I want to say that at the top, because it would be a kind of dishonesty to write about raising daughters as if I had done it. I have not. What I have done is pastor the fathers and mothers of daughters for fifteen years, watch the girls in my congregation grow up inside a machine that means them harm, and raise five boys who are, whether I like it or not, part of the world those girls have to survive. So I write this from beside the problem rather than inside it, and I write it partly as a confession, because the sons I am raising are being formed by the same machine, on the other side of it, to consume what it teaches them to see.

The machine has a name, or several. The academic term is the sexual objectification of women, and the developmental research on it is now substantial enough that I do not have to speculate. The girls in your house are being trained, from an age earlier than you think, to experience themselves as things to be looked at. That is the war. And the church has too often responded to it with a counter-lie that is only the same lie in a longer skirt.

## The name for what is happening to her

In 1997, two psychologists, Barbara Fredrickson and Tomi-Ann Roberts, published a paper in the journal *Psychology of Women Quarterly* that named the mechanism with unusual precision. They called it objectification theory, and its central claim is this: when a culture persistently treats girls and women as bodies to be evaluated by others, the girls internalize the outside gaze. They begin to watch themselves from the outside. They stop asking what does my body feel and start asking what does my body look like to someone watching. Fredrickson and Roberts called this self-objectification, and their research, replicated many times since, linked it to a cluster of afflictions that fall disproportionately on girls: anxiety, depression, disordered eating, and a diminished ability to be present in one's own life because part of the mind is always occupied monitoring one's appearance.

Sit with the horror of that for a moment. A girl learns to spend a permanent fraction of her attention watching herself be watched. She is never fully inside her own experience, because a portion of her is always outside it, checking the picture. And the machine that trains her, the advertising, the algorithms, the pornographic wallpaper of the culture, the filtered images that even her friends are posting, does this to her before she is old enough to name it or resist it. This is not a moral panic. It is measured, published, and replicated developmental psychology, and it describes a genuine assault on the interior life of the girls we are raising.

> She is taught to watch herself being watched, until a part of her is always standing outside her own life, checking the picture. That is not vanity. It is an injury, and it is being inflicted on purpose.

## The church's counter-lie

Here is where I have to turn on my own house, because the church saw this assault and often responded with something that was not the gospel but its counterfeit. It responded with the purity culture of the 1990s and 2000s, and I watched that culture form a generation of girls, and I have since counseled the women it wounded.

The counter-lie went like this. The world says your body is a thing to be looked at and consumed. The church replied: yes, your body is a thing to be looked at, and therefore you must cover it, guard it, and manage it, because it is a stumbling block, a temptation, a danger to the boys around you. Do you hear what happened? The church accepted the world's basic premise, that the girl's value and meaning are located in her body as an object of the male gaze, and then simply reversed the instruction. The world said display it; the church said hide it. But both agreed on the thing that mattered: she is, first and fundamentally, a body that men will look at, and her spiritual task is to manage that looking.

The fruit of this was bitter, and I have tasted it in my office. Women raised in purity culture who could not experience their own bodies as good even inside a marriage the church itself had blessed, because they had been trained to see their bodies as landmines. Women who carried shame for having been looked at, as if the looking were their sin. Women who had been told, in youth group, that their bodies were the reason a boy might fall, which placed on a fourteen-year-old girl the responsibility for the imagination of every boy who saw her. That is a monstrous burden, and it is the same objectification the world practices, baptized and handed back to her as holiness. We did not free her from the gaze. We just added God's name to it.

## What Scripture actually says about the daughter's body

The recovery is not a better modesty policy. It is a different anthropology, and it is right there in the text we claimed to be defending.

The first thing Scripture says about the human body, male and female, is that it was made in the image of God. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). The daughter's body is not first an object of anyone's gaze. It is first an image of God, a bearer of divine likeness, made to be a subject who looks out at the world and acts within it, not primarily an object that is looked at. Every regime that reduces her to a thing to be evaluated, whether it hands her a bikini or a burden of blame, is denying Genesis 1:27, and the church that adopted the world's premise denied it too.

And Scripture is relentless that the value of a person is not in the surface the world evaluates. "Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised" (Proverbs 31:30). Peter writes to women that their true adornment is not the external, the braided hair and the gold, but "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious" (1 Peter 3:3-4). Read that phrase carefully, because purity culture abused it too: *in God's sight*. The verse relocates the audience. The girl trained by the machine performs for the gaze of the watching world. Peter tells her the audience that matters is God, who sees the hidden person and not the surface, and who has already declared her precious before she managed a single thing about her appearance. That is not another instruction about how to be looked at. It is an escape from the whole economy of being looked at.

## What I am trying to do with my sons

I said this was a confession, and here is the confessing part. The war on daughters cannot be won on the daughters' side alone, because half the machine runs through boys, and I am raising five of them. The girls in your congregation will grow up into a world staffed by men, and some of those men will be mine, and the question of whether they consume women as objects or honor them as image-bearers is being decided right now, in my house, on my watch.

So the work I actually control is not the daughters' modesty. It is my sons' vision. I am trying, imperfectly and against the same machine, to raise boys who see a woman as a whole person before they see her as a body, who are not trained by a decade of pornographic saturation to evaluate before they encounter, who understand that the gaze the world taught them is not neutral looking but a habit of consumption that damages the person consumed and hollows out the one consuming. When Jesus said that a man who looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery in his heart (Matthew 5:28), he located the sin where it belongs, in the one doing the looking, not the one being looked at. Purity culture inverted that verse and hung it on the girls. I am trying to hang it back where Christ put it, on the boys, on my boys, where the responsibility actually lives.

## What a father is actually for

I came to faith from atheism, and I was raised without a father, and those two facts collide most sharply for me right here, because I am now the thing I never had, to sons who will help decide how a generation of daughters is treated. A girl raised with a father who delighted in her mind before her appearance, who was interested in what she thought and not merely how she looked, who was safe and present and did not leave, has been handed a set of instruments for detecting the counterfeit long before the counterfeit arrives. She has felt what it is to be loved as a person by a man, and so the man who wants to love her only as a body has a harder time convincing her that consumption is the same as care. She has a reference point. The absence of that reference point is one of the machine's quietest advantages, and I know it from the inside, because I grew up without the male love that would have taught me what love from a man was supposed to feel like.

The research bears this out with unusual consistency, and I state it carefully because the topic is prone to overreach. Studies of paternal involvement, including the work summarized by researchers like Ronald Rohner on the effects of father acceptance and rejection, have found across cultures that a father's warm, engaged presence correlates with better outcomes for daughters in self-image, in the timing and health of their relationships, and in their resistance to exploitation. This is not a promise, and it is not a mechanism a father can operate like a lever, because children are not machines and God is sovereign over ends no parent controls. But it points at something true and old: that the way a girl is treated by the first man who loves her shapes what she will tolerate from the men who come after. The father is a witness. His love is testimony, admitted into evidence long before she can weigh it, about whether a woman is a subject to be known or an object to be used.

God knew this about himself before any of us knew it about our fathers. The name he most insists on, over against every distortion, is Father, and the psalm calls him "Father of the fatherless and protector of widows" precisely at the point where the human father has failed or vanished (Psalm 68:5). I take that verse personally, because I was one of the fatherless it names, and I have staked my life on the claim that the God it describes is real. A daughter whose earthly father fails her, or dies, or was never there, is not therefore doomed, because there is a Father who does not leave, and the church that mediates his love to the fatherless girl is doing the most direct possible work against the machine. But where a human father is present, he is not off the hook. He is on the front line, and most of us do not treat the assignment with the seriousness the girls deserve.

## The weight this leaves

I cannot tell you how to raise your daughter, because I have never raised one, and I distrust the men who write confidently about a war they have only watched. But I can tell you what I have seen from beside it, and I can tell you the one thing I would stake everything on.

Your daughter is being told, by a machine of enormous power and no conscience, that she is a surface. The world says the surface should be displayed. Some of the church said the surface should be hidden. Both were lying to her about the most basic fact of her existence, which is that she is not a surface at all. She is an image of God, a subject with a soul and a will and a mind, made to look out at the world and love it and act in it, precious in God's sight before and beneath and entirely apart from whether anyone ever finds her beautiful. If she believes that, all the way down, the machine loses its grip, because the machine only works on a girl who has agreed to be a surface. And if she does not believe it, no modesty policy in the world will save her, because she will only be a well-covered object instead of an exposed one, still watching herself be watched.

The war for your daughter is not, finally, a war over her clothing. It is a war over whether she is a person or a thing. The world has picked its side. Too often the church, meaning to fight the world, picked the same side in different words. I have five sons and no daughters, and the most useful thing I can do in this war is make sure the men I am sending into it have learned to see a person where the machine trained them to see a thing. That is my part. The daughters are worth every hour of it, and I am not certain we have given them the hours they deserve.

chapters.title: Single Parenting and the Myth of the Complete Family
chapters.summary: The church built a myth of the complete family and then quietly told single parents they had failed to build it. But the God who raised his own people had no such family either.
chapters.body:
I was raised without a father. That fact is not a footnote in my life. It is closer to the center of it, and it shapes how I read every Christian conversation about the family, especially the ones conducted by people who have never known its absence. Because the church I eventually joined had a great deal to say about the family, and much of it, however unintentionally, landed on a boy like me as an indictment. Your family was incomplete. Something was missing. The implied conclusion, never quite spoken but always felt, was that I was missing something too.

I want to write toward the single parents, and toward the children of single parents, and toward a church that has too often handed both a burden dressed up as a doctrine. And I want to do it honestly, which means naming the ways the church built a myth of the complete family and then quietly taxed the people who did not fit it.

## The myth we mistook for the gospel

Somewhere along the way, a particular arrangement of the family, two parents, a mother and a father, children between them, became elevated in the Christian imagination to the status of a near-sacrament. The nuclear family became the assumed default of every sermon, every ministry, every program. And whatever does not fit that shape came to be seen, however gently, as broken, deficient, a deviation from the design.

But this elevation of the nuclear family is not as biblical as we assume. It owes at least as much to a particular era of Western culture as it does to Scripture. The families of the Bible are a chaotic assortment of arrangements, blended and extended and irregular, held together by covenant more than by tidy structure. The people of God were formed not around the nuclear family but around a covenant community that repeatedly extended itself to the widow, the orphan, the stranger, precisely those whom the nuclear-family ideal leaves out. When we made the intact nuclear family the standard, we quietly abandoned the very people Scripture instructs us to gather in.

> The church took a cultural arrangement and baptized it as the divine design, then handed the bill to everyone whose family did not fit the frame. That is not the gospel. That is a preference wearing the gospel's clothing.

The isolated nuclear household, mother and father and children alone in a single dwelling, self-sufficient and turned inward, is a relatively recent development in human history, and a peculiarly modern one at that. For most of human existence, families were embedded in extended networks of kin and community, and children were raised by many hands. When the church made the modern nuclear family the measure of a real family, it did not recover a biblical ideal. It absorbed a cultural accident and gave it the authority of divine command.

## What the myth does to a child

I know what the myth does to a child, because it did it to me. When the entire architecture of your church assumes a father in the home, a boy without one absorbs the message that his family is a problem, that his situation is a deficiency, that he is starting the race behind. No one has to say it. The assumption says it. Every Father's Day sermon that celebrated the family I did not have said it. Every ministry built around a structure my family lacked said it.

And the deeper wound was theological. When I was told that God was a father, the metaphor that was meant to comfort me instead named my wound. The very language the church used to describe God's love was borrowed from the relationship I had been denied. It took me years to understand that God being a father was not an insult to my fatherlessness but its answer, that the God who describes himself as father to the fatherless was speaking directly to a boy like me, offering not a reminder of absence but the promise of a presence that would not leave. But no one framed it that way. The church assumed the earthly father and lost the boy who did not have one.

## To the single parent carrying it alone

If you are a single parent, I want to say something to you that the church has not said often enough. You are not a broken version of a real family. You are a family. Complete, whole, sufficient, held by the God who has always specialized in the family the world calls incomplete. The exhaustion you carry, the double load of being both provider and nurturer, of making every decision without a partner to share the weight, of falling into bed at night with no one to say you did well today, that exhaustion is holy, and it is seen, even when no one around you seems to see it.

The myth of the complete family did not just wound your children. It wounded you, by teaching you to see your own faithful, sacrificial, exhausting love as somehow second-rate. It is not second-rate. The love you pour out, alone, into your children, is as full and as real and as blessed as any love poured out by two. God does not grade families on a curve of structure. God looks at the love, and your love, single parent, is not diminished by the fact that you carry it alone. If anything, it is magnified by the weight you bear to give it.

> Your family is not missing a piece. It is a whole thing, held by a whole God, and the love you give alone is not worth less than the love others give together. The scale God uses does not measure structure. It measures love.

I watched my own mother carry this weight, and I did not understand, as a boy, what it cost her. I understand better now. The single parent lives without the thing every married parent takes for granted, a second set of hands, a second perspective, someone to trade off with when the well runs dry. There is no trading off when you parent alone. The well runs dry and you keep drawing from it anyway, because there is no one else to draw. That is not a lesser love. That is a love that has been tested in a fire most parents never have to enter.

## The community that was supposed to be there

Here is where the church must repent, and where I include myself in the repentance, because I have led churches that did this. When Scripture speaks of the fatherless and the widow, it does not merely offer them a metaphor of divine care. It commands the community to become the answer. The people of God are supposed to be the extended family that surrounds the single parent, that provides the men to mentor the fatherless boy and the women to come alongside the exhausted mother, that fills in what a single parent cannot provide alone, not out of pity but out of covenant.

We have largely failed at this. We built programs for the intact families and left the single parents to fend for themselves, and then we had the audacity to lament the state of the fatherless generation, as though the community bore no responsibility for the fathering it was commanded to provide. If the church took seriously its calling to be the family of the fatherless, single parenting would not carry the isolation it carries. The single parent was never meant to parent alone. The community was supposed to show up. The failure of the child is often, at bottom, the failure of a church that would not become the family it was told to be.

## The father to the fatherless

Let me speak now to the deepest wound, the one I carry myself. To the child raised without a father, or a mother, there is a specific ache that never fully resolves, a hunger for a presence that was not there. I will not pretend the gospel makes that ache disappear. It does not. I still feel it, decades later, in moments I do not expect. But I have come to know something about that ache that changed my relationship to it.

The God who calls himself a father to the fatherless is not offering a metaphor to paper over the wound. He is offering himself as the presence I was denied. Not a replacement that erases the loss, but a companion who enters the loss and refuses to leave. The fatherlessness was real. The presence of God in the fatherlessness was also real. And I have found, over the long years, that the very wound of my father's absence became the place where I learned most deeply what it means to be fathered by God, because I had nowhere else to put the hunger.

I do not say this to romanticize the wound or to suggest that the absence was somehow good. It was not good. A boy should have a father, and the God who calls himself father to the fatherless would be the first to say so, because the very naming of the wound as something God must answer is an admission that the wound should not have been there. But I have learned that God does not waste our wounds. The hunger my father's absence carved into me became a capacity for God, a place already hollowed out and waiting to be filled, and the God who filled it did not fill it in spite of the absence but by way of it. This is the strange grace at the heart of the gospel, that God enters our worst losses not to explain them away but to be present in them, and that the very places where we were most abandoned can become the places where we are most deeply found.

## The temptation to overcompensate

There is a trap that waits for the single parent who has absorbed the myth of the incomplete family, and it is the trap of overcompensation. Believing their child is starting behind, the single parent tries to be both parents at once, to fill every role, to make up by sheer effort for the absence the myth has told them is a deficit. And the effort, however loving, can become its own burden, both for the parent who cannot sustain it and for the child who feels the weight of being someone their parent must heroically compensate for.

You do not have to be two parents. You cannot be, and the attempt to be will exhaust you and communicate to your child that they are a problem being managed rather than a person being loved. What your child needs is not two parents worth of effort from one exhausted person. What they need is one parent who is present, who is at peace, who is not frantically trying to prove that the family is not lacking. A single parent who has made peace with their situation, who is not driven by the shame of the myth, offers their child something far more stabilizing than a parent scrambling to be everything. Let the community be the other hands. Let God be the father to the fatherless. Your job is to be the one parent you are, fully and without shame, and to trust that the rest is held by hands larger than yours.

I have watched single parents pour themselves out until there was nothing left, driven by the fear that any moment of rest, any admission of need, any acknowledgment of their own limits, would confirm the verdict the world had already handed down. This is a cruelty the myth imposes, and it must be resisted, because a depleted parent cannot love well, and a parent who models a life of grinding self-erasure teaches their children that love means the annihilation of the self. It does not. Even God rested. The single parent who guards a measure of rest, who receives help without shame, who tends their own soul as well as their children's, is not failing. They are modeling a sustainable love, a love that can go the distance precisely because it does not pretend to be infinite. Your children do not need a martyr. They need a parent who is still standing years from now, and the way to still be standing is to refuse the myth's demand that you empty yourself completely.

## What I want the single parent to hear

You are not raising broken children in a broken family. You are raising loved children in a family God calls whole. The world's myth of completeness is not the gospel's measure. The gospel measures love, and covenant, and faithfulness, and by every one of those measures your family stands complete before God, whatever it lacks by the world's arithmetic.

And to the church, I say we have a debt to pay. We owe the single parents among us the community we were commanded to provide. We owe the fatherless the fathering the covenant obligates us to supply. We owe every family that does not fit the myth an unlearning of the myth, and a return to the God whose own people were never a tidy nuclear arrangement but a gathered community of the broken, the widowed, the orphaned, and the alone, made whole not by their structure but by the God who dwelt among them. That God dwells among the single-parent family too, and calls it not incomplete, but his own.

chapters.title: The Prodigal Child: Waiting Without Controlling
chapters.summary: The parable is usually preached about the son. But it is really about the father, and the almost unbearable discipline of a love that waits, watches the road, and refuses to chase.
chapters.body:
The parable we call the prodigal son is misnamed. It is not chiefly about the son. It is about the father, and about the almost unbearable discipline of a particular kind of love, a love that lets go, that waits, that watches the road, that does not chase and does not control and does not force the return. If you have a child who has wandered, into rebellion, into a life that breaks your heart, into a distance you cannot close, then this parable is not an inspirational story to you. It is an unbearably accurate description of where you live.

I write as a father who has watched a child walk toward a far country, and who has stood at the window in the way the parable describes, and who has had to learn, against every instinct in my body, the discipline of waiting without controlling. It is the hardest thing love has ever asked of me. And I want to be honest that I have not always done it well, because the temptation to control, to chase, to force the outcome, is nearly overwhelming when the person you love is destroying themselves and you cannot stop them.

## The father who let him go

The first thing the father does in the parable is the thing we least want to notice. He lets the son go. The son demands his inheritance, which in that culture was a shocking insult, essentially wishing the father dead. And the father, who had every right and every power to refuse, gives it. He releases the son to a journey he knows will end in ruin. He does not lock the door. He does not withhold the means. He lets his son walk into the far country with his eyes open, knowing what likely awaits.

This is the part that undoes me, because it runs against everything a protective parent wants to do. We want to prevent the disaster. We want to lock the door, cut off the means, make the destructive choice impossible. And there is a place for boundaries, for refusing to fund a child's self-destruction. But the deeper truth of the parable is that love, real love, does not imprison. The father lets the son go because a son who is not free to leave is not a son but a captive, and a love that will not permit departure is not love but control. The releasing was itself an act of love, though it looked like the opposite, and though it must have cost the father everything.

> A love that will not let your child leave is not love. It is captivity. The father released his son to a journey he knew would end in ruin, because a child who cannot leave cannot ever truly return.

Notice that God parents the same way. From the very beginning, God gives his children a freedom that includes the freedom to walk away, to choose the far country, to squander the inheritance. God does not compel love, because compelled love is not love at all. The whole story of Scripture is the story of a God who lets his people go into their wandering and then pursues them, not by force, but by a love that keeps the way home open. The father in the parable is not being negligent when he releases his son. He is loving him the way God loves us, with a love that respects the terrible dignity of our freedom.

## The discipline of the window

We are told that the father saw the son while he was still a long way off, which means the father was watching. He had not moved on, had not hardened his heart, had not decided the son was dead to him. He was at the window, or on the road, scanning the horizon, keeping vigil for a return that had not come and might never come. This is the posture the parable holds up, and it is a discipline more demanding than either chasing or forgetting.

To chase would be easier in a way, because it would feel like doing something. To forget would be easier too, because it would end the pain of hoping. But the father does neither. He does not chase the son into the far country, dragging him home against his will, which would produce only resentment and another departure. And he does not close his heart and move on, which would mean the son had no home to return to even if he wanted one. He holds the terrible middle ground of active waiting, of a hope that keeps watch without controlling, and this is the exact ground where the parents of prodigals are called to stand.

## Why chasing fails

Every instinct in a loving parent, when a child is destroying themselves, is to chase. To intervene. To manage. To do whatever it takes to force the outcome we know is right. And I have tried it. I have chased. I have managed. I have deployed every tool of persuasion, pressure, and control I possessed. And I have learned, at great cost, that chasing a prodigal almost never works, and often makes it worse.

Chasing fails because it removes from the child the very thing they most need, which is to feel the full weight of their own choices. The son in the parable did not come to himself in his father's house, protected from consequences. He came to himself in the pigsty, at the bottom, having spent everything and hit the floor. It was the consequences, not his father's intervention, that turned him. Every time a parent rushes in to soften the consequences, to rescue the prodigal from the bottom, they may be delaying the very moment of reckoning that alone can produce a genuine return. Love that cannot bear to let a child hit bottom sometimes keeps them from the only thing that could bring them home.

> The son did not come to himself in his father's house. He came to himself in the pigsty. Sometimes the most loving thing a parent can do is stop cushioning the fall that alone can wake their child up.

Chasing fails for another reason too. It communicates to the wandering child that the parent has taken responsibility for a choice that belongs to the child. When a parent chases, pleads, and manages, they take the burden of the outcome onto themselves, and the child feels it, and the child resents it, because no one wants their life to be someone else's project. The paradox is that the more responsibility a parent takes for a prodigal's return, the less the prodigal is able to take responsibility for their own life, and the return, when it comes, must be the prodigal's own act, undertaken in freedom, or it is not a return at all.

## The line between waiting and enabling

I want to be careful here, because the discipline of waiting can be counterfeited by mere passivity, and worse, by enabling. There is a difference between waiting for a prodigal to come to themselves and funding the far country. The father gave the son his inheritance and then let him spend it and hit bottom. He did not send monthly checks to sustain the son's life in the pigsty. He did not keep the destruction comfortable.

This is a crucial and painful distinction. Some parents, unable to bear the sight of their child's suffering, keep intervening in ways that remove the natural consequences and thereby prolong the very destruction they grieve. They pay the debts, cover the failures, cushion every fall, and in doing so they keep their child from ever reaching the bottom where the turning happens. This is not the patient love of the father. It is a fear dressed up as love, and it can trap a child in the far country indefinitely. Real waiting sometimes requires the agonizing discipline of letting your child feel the full weight of a life you would give anything to spare them.

The hardest part of this distinction is that it cannot be reduced to a formula. There is no rule that tells you exactly when help is genuine love and when it is enabling, when a boundary is faithful and when it is punitive, when to step in and when to stand back. Every prodigal is different, every situation is different, and the discernment required is agonizing precisely because the stakes are so high and the line is so unclear. What I can say is that the question to ask is not whether an intervention would relieve your child's suffering in the moment, but whether it would serve their turning in the long run. Sometimes relieving the suffering short-circuits the very reckoning that could save them. Sometimes it is exactly the help they need to survive long enough to turn. Only love, prayerful and honest and willing to be wrong, can tell the difference, and even then it will get it wrong sometimes, and will have to trust the God who works through our mistakes as well as our wisdom.

## The running father

And then, when the son does return, the father runs. This detail would have scandalized the original hearers, because a dignified man of that culture did not run, did not hike up his robes and sprint down the road like a boy. But the father runs, abandoning his dignity, covering the distance himself, reaching the son before the son can finish the rehearsed speech of repentance. He does not wait for the full apology. He does not extract the groveling. He runs, and embraces, and restores, before a word of the confession is complete.

This is the heart of the thing, and it is what makes the waiting bearable. The father waits not with a cold heart, keeping score, preparing his conditions for the son's return. He waits with a heart so ready to forgive that the moment the son appears, all the waiting collapses into running. The waiting was never resentment. It was love holding itself in readiness, love keeping the door open and the heart soft, so that when the moment came, there was no barrier, no lecture, no probation, only embrace. The parent of a prodigal must wait with that kind of heart, a heart that is not hardening in the waiting but softening, so that the return, whenever it comes, meets running rather than judgment.

## The elder brother in the mirror

There is a second son in the parable, and we forget him at our peril, because he is often the one the parent of a prodigal most resembles without knowing it. The elder brother never left, never squandered, never wandered. And when the younger son returned to celebration, the elder brother was furious, standing outside the party, refusing to come in, nursing a resentment built on years of dutiful compliance that had never softened into love. He had stayed in the house, but his heart had never been in the same place as his father's.

The danger for the faithful parent of a prodigal is to become the elder brother, to let the years of grief harden into a resentment that poisons the very welcome the returning child would need. To keep a mental ledger of the wrongs done, the pain caused, the years wasted, and to stand ready, when the child returns, not to run but to demand an accounting. If your heart is hardening in the waiting, if your grief is curdling into bitterness, if you find yourself unable to imagine celebrating a return you have decided the child does not deserve, then the parable has a word for you as sharp as any it has for the prodigal. Do not become the elder brother. Keep your heart soft. The father in the story loved both sons, and both sons needed to come home, and one of them was standing in the yard the whole time, lost in plain sight.

## The waiting that has no guarantee

I have to end honestly, because the parable ends with a return, and not every real story does. Some prodigals come home. Some do not, at least not in the time their parents are given to see. And the discipline of waiting without controlling is hardest of all when there is no guarantee, when you keep the door open for years with no sign of return, when you watch the road and the road stays empty.

What I have come to believe, in that hardest place, is that the waiting itself is faithful whether or not it is rewarded in this life. The father's love was not made valid by the son's return. It was valid in the waiting, in the keeping vigil, in the refusal to harden. Even had the son never come back, the father's love would have been no less real, no less an image of the God who waits for all of us with a patience that outlasts our wandering. So keep watching the road. Keep your heart soft. Refuse both the chasing that controls and the forgetting that hardens. And trust that the God who is himself the waiting Father loves your prodigal more than you do, and is watching a road you cannot see, with a patience deeper than yours, ready to run.

chapters.title: The Youth Pastor Who Stopped Believing
chapters.summary: He led the retreats, wrote the talks, and prayed the prayers, and somewhere in the middle of it all the belief drained out of him. This is for the one still standing on the stage after the faith has gone.
chapters.body:
He came to my office on a Tuesday, which is the day pastors have their honest conversations, because Sunday is too raw and Monday is too tired. He was a youth pastor at a church across town, twenty-eight years old, and he told me that he did not believe anymore and he did not know how to stop performing that he did. He had a retreat in three weeks. He had forty teenagers who thought he was the most solid Christian they knew. And he had nothing left inside him but the muscle memory of belief.

I did not tell him what he expected me to tell him. He expected me to fix it, or to fire him in my heart, or to hand him a book of apologetics and send him home. What I told him was that he had just described the loneliest position in the church, and that I was not going to make it worse by pretending it was simple. The youth pastor who stops believing is not a rare defect. He is a common casualty of a system that asks young men to be spiritual professionals before they have been spiritual adults, and then acts shocked when the professional performance outlasts the belief that was supposed to fund it.

## How the Faith Drained Out Without a Single Argument

Here is what surprised me most as he talked. There was no argument that broke him. He had not read the New Atheists and been convinced. He had not encountered a suffering he could not square with God. What had happened was slower and more corrosive than that. He had spent six years talking about God for a living, and somewhere in the talking, God had become a subject rather than a person. He had produced so many words about faith that he had used up his own.

The sociologist Christian Smith, in his 2005 study Soul Searching, coined a term for the actual religion of American teenagers. He called it moralistic therapeutic deism, a faith in a God who wants you to be nice, to feel good, and to stay largely out of your business until you need him. Smith's point that stung me was that the teenagers learned this faith from the adults. And the youth pastor is the front line of that transmission. He is handed a curriculum built to keep teenagers comfortable and mildly moral, and he is asked to be personally on fire for a God the curriculum has already reduced to a life coach. Of course the fire goes out. You cannot burn on fumes.

I asked him what he actually preached to the teenagers. He described talks about identity, about not comparing yourself to others, about God having a wonderful plan. I asked him when he had last preached the cross, the actual scandal of a God who died. He could not remember. He had been feeding teenagers spiritual snacks for years, and he had been living on the same snacks, and a man cannot survive on snacks. Neither can a faith. This was not primarily a crisis of belief. It was a crisis of malnourishment that had presented as a crisis of belief.

## The Machine That Manufactures This Failure

I want to indict a system, and I want to indict myself as part of it, because I have hired youth pastors and handed them the same impossible assignment. The modern youth ministry model asks a young man in his twenties, often with no seminary training and little life experience, to be simultaneously an entertainer, a counselor, an event planner, a theologian, and a spiritual exemplar to thirty or forty teenagers who are watching him for signs that this whole thing is real. We pay him poorly, work him seventy hours a week, evaluate him by attendance numbers, and then we are surprised when the man cracks. We built the machine that broke him, and then we blame him for breaking.

The historian and pastor Eugene Peterson warned about this in his 1992 book Under the Unpredictable Plant, where he described how the pastoral vocation gets deformed into what he called religious careerism, the pastor turned into a manager of religious goods and services, measured by the growth of the enterprise rather than the depth of souls. Peterson saw that this deformation was spiritually lethal, because it required the pastor to perform a vitality he was too busy to actually possess. The youth pastor is the most exposed position in this whole system, because he works with the age group most sensitive to hypocrisy, and he must perform the most and is given the least to perform from. The wonder is not that some of them stop believing. The wonder is that any of them survive with a faith intact.

So when the man sat across from me, I did not see a spiritual failure. I saw a casualty of a machine that had used him up and would use up the next one just the same. And the first pastoral act was to tell him that, to lift the private shame off him and name the systemic thing that had ground him down. He had thought his emptiness was a moral failure, a sign that he was secretly a fraud. It was nothing of the kind. It was the predictable result of asking a man to give out water faster than anyone ever let him take any in.

## The Difference Between Belief and Employment

The cruelest part of his situation was the entanglement of his faith with his paycheck. When an ordinary Christian doubts, they can sit in the back and say nothing and let the doubt run its course. When a youth pastor doubts, doubting means losing his income, his housing sometimes, his community entirely, and his identity as the person everyone counts on. So the pressure is enormous to fake it, and the faking accelerates the very death he is afraid of, because nothing kills faith faster than performing a faith you do not have.

> "Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness." (James 3:1)

I read him that verse, and I told him it was not a threat. It was a mercy. James is warning that the position of the teacher is dangerous, that it carries a weight the ordinary believer does not carry. If James thought teaching was spiritually hazardous in the first century, how much more in a system that turns twenty-two-year-olds into spiritual authorities before they have suffered anything, before they have doubted anything, before they have had a faith tested enough to know whether it holds. The youth pastor who stops believing is not failing at an easy job. He is being crushed by a hard one that everyone pretends is easy.

## What I Know About Standing on a Stage Empty

I came to faith from atheism, so I know the emptiness he described from the inside, but I know something else too. I have stood in a pulpit on a Sunday when I did not feel a thing, when the words came out of my mouth and I wondered if I meant them, when the congregation received a comfort I could not locate in myself. Every honest pastor has stood there. And the question that saved me, the question I gave him, was this. Is the truth of the gospel dependent on my current feeling of it, or is my feeling of it downstream of something that stays true whether I feel it or not.

Because if the gospel is true, it does not become false when I stop feeling it. The resurrection either happened in history around the year 30 or it did not, and my emotional state in 2026 does not vote on the matter. This is the great relief of a faith anchored in event rather than experience. My experience of the risen Christ can fail entirely, and the risen Christ is not thereby diminished. The scholar N.T. Wright spent seven hundred pages in his 2003 work The Resurrection of the Son of God making the historical case that something happened to the disciples that a hallucination cannot explain and a legend cannot account for. That case does not weaken when a youth pastor feels nothing. The object of faith and the feeling of faith are not the same object, and confusing them is what breaks men.

## The Path That Is Not Deconstruction and Not Denial

He wanted to know his options, and he had reduced them to two. He could keep faking it, which was killing him, or he could blow up his life, quit, tell everyone, and start over as an unbeliever. I told him there was a third door, and it was the hardest and the only one worth walking through. He could stop faking, tell the truth to the right people, and let his faith be rebuilt from a foundation deeper than the youth ministry industrial complex had ever given him.

The first move was to tell the truth to someone with authority over him who would not fire him for honesty. This is the tragedy. Most youth pastors do not have such a person, because the system punishes exactly the honesty it most needs. So sometimes the right person is outside the employing church, a pastor across town, a counselor, a spiritual director who has walked men through this before. He needed to say the true sentence out loud to a safe person, because a doubt spoken to a trusted human loses half its terror, and a doubt kept secret grows in the dark until it swallows everything.

The second move was to stop producing words about God long enough to receive some. He needed a sabbatical from the stage, even a short one, because you cannot fill a bucket that is pouring out faster than you pour in. Eugene Peterson wrote in his 1987 book Working the Angles that the pastor's real work is prayer, Scripture, and spiritual direction, and that everything else is running the church rather than being a pastor. Peterson's warning was that pastors get so busy with the machinery of religion that they starve at the very well they are supposed to be tending. My friend had been running the machine for six years and had not drawn a bucket for himself in as long. No wonder he was dry.

## Rebuilding on the Older Ground

The faith he had was not deep enough to lose. That sounds harsh. I mean it as hope. What drained out of him was a thin, therapeutic, experience-dependent Christianity that was never going to survive contact with real life. Its draining was not a tragedy. It was a clearing. Under the thin thing was the possibility of the older thing, the creedal faith the church has held for two thousand years, tested by persecution and plague and every argument the human mind has thrown at it. He had never actually stood on that ground. He had stood on the youth-camp version of it, and the youth-camp version cannot hold the weight of a grown man.

So I did not tell him to work up his old feelings. I told him to read the people who had faith under fire. Bonhoeffer writing from a Nazi prison. Augustine writing his Confessions in the fourth century about his own long unbelief and the God who chased him down. The Psalms, which contain more doubt per page than most sermons contain in a year. I told him to let the thin faith die and to see whether, in its death, he found himself standing on something that had been under it the whole time. That is not deconstruction, which takes the faith apart and stops. It is reconstruction, which digs down to the load-bearing ground and builds there.

## A Word to the One Reading This on the Stage

If you are the youth pastor, or the worship leader, or the small-group host, and you have been performing a faith that left you months ago, hear this. You are not a fraud in the way you fear. A fraud never believed. You believed, and you are grieving, and grief and fraud are not the same sin. But you cannot keep performing, because the performance is the poison. It is time to tell someone the truth.

And if the emptiness has become something darker, if you have started to feel that the whole thing was a lie and that you would be better off gone, do not carry that in silence for one more night. That thought is not the truth telling you something. It is the exhaustion lying to you in the voice of clarity. Call someone tonight. A friend, a pastor, a counselor, a crisis line. The despair wants you alone, because it can only win in isolation. Deny it the isolation and you have already begun to deny it the victory.

## The Verdict

The youth pastor who stopped believing did not lose the faith. He lost the counterfeit that had been standing in for it, and the loss felt like the end because he had never known there was anything underneath. There was. There always is. The God who found me in atheism is not smaller than the disappointment of a burned-out twenty-eight-year-old. He is not threatened by the honesty. He is waiting on the far side of it.

Get off the stage long enough to be found. Tell the truth to someone who will not punish you for it. And let the thin thing die so the real thing can come up under your feet. The retreat in three weeks is not more important than your soul. Cancel it if you have to. God can raise up someone to give the talk. He cannot easily raise up a man who spent his whole life performing a faith he never got to actually have.

chapters.title: When Your Child Comes Out
chapters.summary: The moment your child comes out, everything you believe meets everyone you love, and the two seem to collide. What matters most in that moment is whether the relationship survives it.
chapters.body:
This is among the hardest subjects I could write about, and I want to be honest at the outset about why. It is hard because it touches convictions people hold deeply and disagree about sharply, and because whatever I say, some will feel I have said too much and others too little. But it is hard most of all because it is not, in the moment it actually happens, an abstract debate about theology. It is a child, your child, standing in front of you, having gathered every ounce of their courage to tell you something true about themselves, watching your face to see what happens next.

I am a pastor with settled theological convictions, and I am not going to pretend I do not have them. But I have also sat with too many families in the aftermath of that moment, watched too many relationships shatter and a few survive, to believe that the most important thing in that moment is winning a theological argument. I want to write about what happens when your child comes out, and about the difference between what you believe and how you love, and about why the relationship must survive whatever else is true.

## The moment before the moment

By the time a child tells you, they have usually been carrying it, alone, for a long time. Often years. They have rehearsed the conversation a hundred times, imagined every reaction, braced for rejection. What you are seeing when they finally speak is not an impulsive announcement but the end of a long and lonely internal ordeal, and the courage it took to speak is enormous, especially in a home where they have reason to fear the response.

This matters because it should reframe how we understand the moment. Your child is not attacking your beliefs. They are trusting you with the most vulnerable truth about themselves, at real risk, hoping against their fear that your love is bigger than whatever they expect your judgment to be. And the first thing they will learn, in the first seconds of your response, is whether that hope was justified. Long before any conversation about theology, they will read your face and know whether they are still safe with you. That reading happens before a word is spoken, and it may determine everything that follows.

> Your child did not come to debate you. They came to be known by you, at the risk of being rejected by you. The first thing they will learn from your response is not what you believe. It is whether they are still safe.

Consider what it took for them to reach this moment. Consider the nights they lay awake wondering whether telling you would cost them your love. Consider that they chose you, chose to risk it, chose to bring you into the truth rather than hiding it from you forever. That choice is itself an act of trust and of love, an offering, and how you receive it will tell your child, more than any words, whether the trust was well placed. The moment is not primarily a test of your theology. It is a test of your love, and your child already knows which one they are hoping to find.

## The distinction that saves relationships

There is a distinction that I have come to believe is the difference between families that survive this moment and families that do not. It is the distinction between what you believe and how you love. These are not the same thing, and the great error of the anxious parent is to collapse them, to believe that loving their child requires either abandoning their convictions or enforcing them, when in fact love and conviction operate on different planes entirely.

Consider how God relates to every one of us. God holds convictions about how we ought to live that not one of us fully meets, and yet God's love for us is not withdrawn pending our compliance. God does not make his welcome conditional on our getting everything right first. The gospel is precisely that we are loved before we are fixed, welcomed before we are worthy, embraced in the midst of everything about us that falls short. If God, who has every right to make love conditional on agreement, does not do so, then a parent has no ground to make their love for their child conditional on the child's agreement with them.

You can hold your convictions and love your child without condition at the same time. In fact, you must, because that is exactly how you yourself are loved by God. The parent who says I cannot love you fully unless you agree with me has departed from the gospel they claim to defend, and has substituted for it a conditional love that the God of the gospel never once showed them. The whole scandal of grace is that God's love reaches us in the middle of our disagreement with him, and does not wait for us to come around before it embraces us.

## What rejection actually accomplishes

Let me speak plainly about what happens when a parent responds to a child coming out with rejection, with coldness, with the ultimatum that the relationship is contingent on the child changing. It does not accomplish what the parent hopes. It does not draw the child toward the parent's convictions. It does the opposite. It drives the child away, not only from the parent but very often from the faith the parent holds, because the child now associates that faith with the rejection they experienced from the person who was supposed to love them most.

I have watched this happen more times than I can bear to remember. A parent, acting out of what they believed was faithfulness, rejected a child, and in doing so taught the child that the God of that parent was a God of rejection, and the child walked away from both. The rejection did not protect the child's soul. It endangered it. It took whatever openness the child might have retained toward faith and slammed it shut, and it did so in the name of the very faith it destroyed. Whatever you believe about the questions involved, rejection is a catastrophic strategy, and it fails on its own terms.

> Rejection does not draw a child toward your convictions. It drives them away from you and from the God you hoped they would find, and it does its damage in the name of the very faith it destroys.

The statistics on what happens to young people rejected by their families are grim, and I will not sensationalize them, but neither will I hide from them. A young person who loses their family's love in the moment they most needed it does not simply lose a relationship. They lose a foundation, and the loss reverberates into every corner of their life and their faith. If we say we care about our children's souls, then we must reckon with the fact that rejection is among the surest ways to imperil the very soul we claim to be protecting.

## The relationship must survive

If I could say one thing to a parent in the moment their child comes out, it would be this: whatever else happens, the relationship must survive. Not because the relationship is more important than truth, but because the relationship is the only vessel in which anything true can be received. A child who is cut off cannot hear anything you have to say. A child who remains in relationship with you, who knows your love is durable, who trusts that you will not abandon them, remains someone with whom every conversation is still possible.

The father in the parable did not stand at the edge of the property and shout his convictions at the departing son. He let the relationship hold across the distance, kept the door open, watched the road, and when the son returned, he ran. The whole possibility of that reunion depended on the father not burning the relationship down in the name of being right. Keep the relationship alive. Keep the door open. Whatever you believe, do not let your convictions become the reason your child is no longer in your life, because a child you have lost is a child you can no longer love in any way that reaches them.

## The temptation to make it about you

I have to name something uncomfortable, because it is true and because avoiding it would be dishonest. When a child comes out, many parents make the moment about themselves. About their disappointment. About their reputation. About the future they had imagined. About what people at church will think. And the child, who came to be known and loved, instead finds themselves managing their parent's grief, apologizing for the pain they have caused, comforting the very person who was supposed to comfort them.

This is a failure of love, and I say that as someone who understands the parent's genuine grief. Your feelings are real, and they deserve a place to be processed, but that place is not in front of your child in the moment of their vulnerability. To make their coming out about your loss is to abandon them in the moment they most needed to be received. There will be time to work through your own response, with God and with trusted others. In the moment itself, the work is to receive your child, to communicate that they are loved and safe, to keep your own grief from becoming a burden you lay on the shoulders of a child who is already carrying enough.

I want to be careful and compassionate here, because I am not saying your grief is illegitimate. If you had imagined a certain future for your child, and that future is now shifting, you may feel a genuine loss, and that loss is real, and pretending it away helps no one. But grief has an appropriate place and an inappropriate one, and the appropriate place is not on the shoulders of the child who has just entrusted you with their truth. Take your grief to God. Take it to a friend, a counselor, a pastor who can hold it. Do the work of examining it, of asking how much of it is genuine loss and how much is wounded expectation, disappointed image, fear of what others will think. But do that work away from your child, so that when you are with your child, what they encounter is not your grief but your love. The order matters enormously. Receive first. Grieve elsewhere. Return to your child with a love that has done its own work and is therefore free to be wholly about them.

## The long view of the relationship

One of the traps in this moment is to treat it as a single decisive event, a fork in the road where everything is settled once and for all. It is not. The moment your child comes out is the beginning of a relationship that will unfold over years and decades, and the pressure to resolve everything in the first conversation is a pressure to force what only time can work out. You do not have to have all your responses figured out. You do not have to deliver a definitive statement of where you stand. In the moment, you have to love, and to keep loving, and to leave the longer conversations for the longer relationship.

Parents who survive this well tend to be the ones who took the long view, who resisted the urge to make the first conversation carry all the weight, who trusted that a relationship kept warm over years has room for many conversations, many disagreements, many gradual understandings. The child who knows they are loved does not need every question answered on the first night. They need to know the relationship will hold, that there will be a second conversation and a hundredth, that they have not lost their parent by telling the truth. Give the relationship time. The things that cannot be resolved in a moment can often be held, together, over a lifetime, if the relationship is allowed to survive the moment.

## Holding conviction with humility

For those who hold traditional convictions, and I do not hide that I count myself among those who take Scripture's teaching seriously, there is a way to hold conviction that leaves room for love, and a way that does not. Conviction held with humility remembers that the person holding it is also a sinner in need of grace, is also someone who falls short of what they believe, is also loved by God in the midst of their own failures. Conviction held with humility does not weaponize itself against a child.

The parent who approaches their child from a posture of moral superiority, who treats their conviction as a stone to throw rather than a burden they too carry, has misunderstood the gospel entirely. We are all people who fall short. The parent stands before God on exactly the same ground as the child, both of them recipients of a grace neither has earned. To love your child while holding your convictions is not compromise. It is simply to treat your child the way God has treated you, which is to say, with a love that precedes and outlasts every question about whether they have gotten everything right. Hold what you believe. But hold your child first, and hold them always, and never let go.

chapters.title: When Your Child Doubts or Walks Away
chapters.summary: The day your child tells you he no longer believes is not the day your faith failed, and the worst thing you can do in that moment is to make him choose between his honesty and your love.
chapters.body:
There is a particular silence that falls in a Christian home when a child says, for the first time and meaning it, that he is not sure he believes any of this anymore. I have sat with parents in that silence many times, and I have felt the early tremor of it in my own house, and I can tell you that almost everything a parent instinctively does in that moment makes it worse. The instinct is to argue, to fix, to panic, to grieve out loud in a way that lands on the child as accusation. The instinct is to treat the doubt as an emergency to be ended rather than a person to be heard. And the child, watching the parent's face fall, learns the lesson that will shape everything after: that his honesty has cost him, that the price of telling the truth in this family is the look that just crossed his father's face.

So before anything else, before a single argument or resource or strategy, the parent must do the hardest thing, which is to not flinch. Your child has just handed you the most fragile and honest thing he has, and the very first thing he is measuring is whether he is still safe with you. If your response teaches him that doubt makes him an outsider in his own home, he will take his doubt and his eventual conclusions somewhere else, somewhere you cannot follow, and you will have traded a hard conversation now for a closed door later. The flinch is the thing that does the damage. Not the doubt. The flinch.

Let me steel-man the walking away, because the parent who cannot understand why a thoughtful young person leaves the faith is a parent who will only ever be talking past his own child. Many who leave do not leave because they were seduced by sin or never really believed, which is the comforting story we tell because it absolves us. Many leave because they took the faith seriously and ran into something they could not square. They saw the church protect an abuser. They watched believers they trusted baptize cruelty in religious language. They asked an honest question at fourteen and got a defensive non answer that taught them the adults were afraid of the question, which a child correctly reads as evidence the adults are not sure of their own ground. They encountered the problem of suffering not as a philosophy seminar but as a friend's funeral. These are not flimsy reasons. Some of them are the same reasons that nearly took my own faith, back when I was the atheist and not the pastor, and I will not insult my children by pretending their doubts are smaller than the ones I had. To do so would be to forget where I came from.

This is the part of my own story that matters here and the only part I will tell, because it is the part that disqualifies me from panicking. I did not grow up believing and lose it. I grew up with nothing and was found, and that means I know from the inside that the road back is real, that a person can stand exactly where my child is standing and not stay there forever. I cannot use that to make any promises, because my road is not my child's road and grace is not a formula. But it does mean I am physically incapable of believing that the door is closed, because I walked through it myself from the other side. A parent who has only ever believed may experience a child's doubt as the end of the world. A parent who was once the doubter knows it is a country, not a cliff, and people come home from countries.

Now the practical, because compassion without wisdom just becomes a warm puddle. First, distinguish what kind of doubt you are dealing with, because they are not all the same and they do not all want the same response. Intellectual doubt asks real questions and wants real answers, and the worst thing you can do is hand it a slogan. If your child has a genuine question about the reliability of the texts or the problem of evil or the morality of the Old Testament, then take the question seriously enough to find a serious answer, even if that means saying you do not know and going to find someone who has thought harder than you have. There are people who have spent their lives on exactly these questions. Hand your child the strong version of the answer, not the version that only works if he does not push on it. A child can smell a fragile answer, and a fragile answer confirms his fear that the whole thing is fragile.

There is a temptation hiding inside even the good practice of taking questions seriously, and it is the temptation to win. You go and find the strong answer, you bring it home, you lay it out, and somewhere in the laying out your child can feel that you are not exploring the question with him, you are defeating it, and by extension defeating him. The posture matters more than the content. A father who comes to his doubting child as a prosecutor with a closing argument has already lost, even if every point is correct, because the child did not come for a verdict, he came to find out if he could think out loud in your presence and still be safe.
